label: A statutory provision should be interpreted in context, by reading it together with related provisions in the same statute and considering the structure and interrelationship of the parts as a whole.
A statute should be construed in light of its purpose.
If statutory language is plain, it should be applied according to its plain terms.
Courts should not read into a statute a requirement or limitation that the statute does not mention.
The legislative history of a statute can be used to interpret its provisions.
A statute should be interpreted in a way that gives effect to all its provisions, ensuring that no part is rendered inoperative or superfluous.

When Congress includes particular language in one section of a statute but omits it in another section of the same Act, it is generally presumed that Congress acts intentionally and purposely in the disparate inclusion or exclusion.

Statutes that are part of the same legislative scheme or address similar subject matter should be construed in pari materia, meaning they should be interpreted together to achieve a coherent and consistent legislative framework.
When Congress reenacts or recodifies statutory language without material change, the provision is generally presumed to retain its prior meaning and effect.
When interpreting statutes, courts should use ordinary meaning.
When a statute expressly defines a term, that definition governs the meaning of the term as used in the statute.
The expressio unius canon: The inclusion of certain items in a statute implies the exclusion of others not mentioned.
A statute should not be interpreted in a way that leads to absurd results.
Repeals by implication are disfavored; courts should not treat a later statute as implicitly repealing an earlier one absent a clear indication that Congress intended repeal.
Courts may give interpretive weight to an agency’s consistent, contemporaneous, long-standing construction of a statute.
Statutory language should be construed in its context—reading words and phrases in light of surrounding text and their antecedents—rather than in isolation.
Courts may consult dictionaries as evidence of the meaning of statutory words or phrases.
If a statute is fairly susceptible to an interpretation that avoids serious constitutional questions, courts should adopt that interpretation.
If statutory text is amenable to more than one plausible interpretation, a court should prefer the interpretation that avoids serious anomalies or unreasonable practical results.
Following statutory stare decisis, courts generally should adhere to prior judicial interpretations of a statute.
When a specific statutory provision conflicts with a more general provision, the specific provision controls.
When Congress amends statutory language, the change in text is generally taken to reflect an intent to change the law’s meaning.
Statutes in derogation of the common law are strictly construed; courts do not read a statute to abrogate or displace established common-law rules or rights absent a clear indication.
In areas of traditional state police powers, a federal statute should not be read to preempt state law unless Congress has made that intent clear and manifest.
Identical words or phrases used in the same statute are generally presumed to carry the same meaning.
Courts apply a presumption against ineffectiveness and avoid interpretations that would render a statute or provision useless or ineffectual.
When a statute uses a term with an established common law meaning, it is presumed that Congress intended to adopt the common law definition.
When interpreting a statutory term or phrase, courts may look to judicial interpretations of the same or similar language in other statutes as a guide to its meaning.
When a statute uses a familiar legal expression, it is presumed to carry its familiar legal meaning.
A statute's title or headings may be consulted to resolve ambiguity or confirm a reading, but it cannot override the statute's text.

When statutory text is clear, courts should enforce it according to its terms and should not adopt implausible or atextual constructions (including saving constructions) that effectively rewrite the statute.
Statutory provisions should be interpreted, where possible, in harmony so that each can operate without negating the other.
When Congress uses a statutory term against a backdrop of a settled judicial understanding, Congress is presumed to adopt the term's settled meaning.

Where a statute (or similar enacted legal text) expressly limits its scope, interpreters should apply it only within those stated limits and not extend it to subjects outside the text’s defined coverage.
Statutory interpretation begins with the text of the statute.
Courts should construe exceptions to a general statutory requirement narrowly.
Statutes are presumed not to apply retroactively.
Courts may not rewrite statutes based on judges' views about wise policy.
Courts should defer to an agency's reasonable interpretation of a statute it administers unless that interpretation is inconsistent with the clear intent of Congress.
Longstanding interpretations and applications of a statute are strong evidence of its meaning.
When a statute expressly enumerates specific exemptions or exceptions, courts generally should not create additional implied exceptions beyond those Congress provided.
A statute applies only when its textually specified conditions or triggers are satisfied.
Legislative history should not control over enacted text.
When Congress uses the same words in closely related statutes courts generally presume the words have the same meaning in both statutes.
Courts generally should not rely on post-enactment legislative history to discern the enacting legislature's understanding.
When interpreting a state statute, a federal court is bound by the state courts’ authoritative construction of that statute (especially the state’s highest court).
When a statute uses "shall," it ordinarily imposes a mandatory duty, and when it uses "may," it ordinarily confers discretion.
Rule of lenity: Ambiguity in a statute defining a crime should be resolved in the defendant's favor.
When two plausible statutory interpretations would be constitutional and unconstitutional respectively, courts should adopt the constitutional interpretation.
The noscitur a sociis canon states that a word is known by the company it keeps, meaning that the meaning of a word should be determined by considering the surrounding words and context.
Courts may rely on subsequent amendments as clarifying evidence of original statute's meaning.
Remedial legislation should be construed liberally to advance the remedy and accomplish its evident remedial purpose.
A statutory proviso is ordinarily read as a qualification or limitation on the preceding clause or section, rather than as an expansive, independent grant or rule.
When a statute uses mandatory terms such as 'must' or 'shall,' courts ordinarily presume the requirement is mandatory.
Statutory terms should not be construed in a way that would undermine or defeat the statute's evident design or allow parties to circumvent it.
Statutory terms connected by the disjunctive “or” are ordinarily read to provide alternatives.
When a statute specifies an exclusive procedure or enforcement method, courts should assume Congress intended to preclude other procedures or enforcement methods.
Courts may consult a statute's earlier versions and statutory precursors to help determine the meaning of the current provision.
Statutory language should be interpreted in light of the relevant historical and legal backdrop.
Statutes are not construed to waive sovereign immunity unless the waiver is unequivocally expressed in the statutory text, and any waiver is strictly construed in favor of the sovereign.

A statute’s findings, statements of objectives, and declared purposes may be consulted as context to illuminate the statute’s focus and aims (and thus help resolve interpretive uncertainty), but they do not override clear operative text.
Statutes are interpreted against the backdrop of existing common-law and general legal principles, which inform statutory meaning unless the text indicates otherwise.
Under the ejusdem generis canon, when a general term follows a list of specific terms, the general term is interpreted to include only items of the same type as those listed.
Inferences about an enacted statute's meaning drawn from unenacted bill versions or rejected legislative proposals are, at most, weak.
Congress does not make major changes to a statutory scheme or to fundamental legal rules through vague terms or ancillary provisions; a change of that magnitude requires a clear statement.
A later-enacted statute can modify, qualify, or supersede the operation of an earlier statute addressing the same subject matter (a later-in-time enactment may control over inconsistent earlier law).

Even when a case falls within a statute’s literal terms, courts may decline to apply the statute to that case when doing so would contravene the statute’s spirit or clearly ascertainable purpose or intent of its makers.
Constitutional avoidance does not authorize courts to rewrite the statute or adopt an implausible reading.
Courts should not imply a statutory private cause of action or additional remedy without evidence that Congress intended to provide it.
A longstanding judicial interpretation of a statutory scheme that Congress leaves undisturbed may suggest that Congress has acquiesced in that interpretation.
Legislative (including drafting) history is of limited interpretive value and should be used with caution.
When a statute incorporates another statute by reference, the provisions of the incorporated statute are applied as if they were part of the incorporating statute.

A long-continued administrative construction of a statute, followed by Congress’s repeated reenactment of the relevant language without change, is strong evidence of (and may control) the statute’s meaning.
Statutory terms are ordinarily given their common, everyday meaning, read in context, unless the statute indicates a technical or specialized usage.
Courts should interpret broad, unqualified terms according to their ordinary scope and should not imply limitations.
Statutory language is interpreted according to its ordinary meaning at the time of enactment.

Judicial review (and related access to court) is presumed available; a statute will not be read to preclude or cut off judicial review unless there is a persuasive indication that Congress intended that result.
When a statute grants power or authority to accomplish an end, it generally includes the incidental powers necessary to make that grant effective, absent contrary indication.
Courts presume Congress legislates with awareness of existing law and relevant judicial decisions.
In determining whether an action falls within a statutory category, courts may look to the action’s substance and practical operation (its form or function), rather than relying solely on its label.

When Congress considers and rejects statutory language that would have produced a particular result, that rejection is strong evidence against interpreting the enacted statute to produce that rejected result.
When Congress explicitly states that a statute does not affect existing legal protections or authorities, it is presumed that those protections or authorities remain intact.

A statute should not be narrowly limited to the particular applications or situations that legislators specifically contemplated at enactment; its general terms may extend to unforeseen circumstances.
Courts should not treat a statutory requirement as jurisdictional absent a clear indication from Congress in text or context.

Courts may give agency interpretations Skidmore weight—i.e., give it respect proportional to its persuasiveness, including factors such as the agency’s expertise, consistency, and the thoroughness/care reflected in the interpretation.

The enumeration of specified items or grounds in a statute does not necessarily imply the exclusion of other items or grounds not mentioned (i.e., a negative implication from enumeration is not automatic).
Legislative (congressional) intent must be grounded primarily in the statute’s text (and structure); a statute’s remedial purpose cannot justify departing from the limits of the enacted language.
When Congress omits or deletes specific language during enactment, that history may provide limited evidence of an intent not to adopt the omitted provision.
Absent a clear indication to the contrary, statutes are presumed not to apply extraterritorially.
Statutory provisions authorizing appeals (or otherwise conferring appellate jurisdiction) are to be strictly construed and not expanded beyond their clear terms.
The absence of language indicating exclusivity in a statute suggests that the statute is not intended to be the sole means of regulation or protection.
Later legislation may be cited as evidence of Congress’s acquiescence to an existing understanding of an earlier statutory scheme.
When statutory context indicates Congress used a technical term or term of art, courts interpret it in its technical sense as used in the relevant field (often confirmed by professional usage).
A statute should not be interpreted as displacing courts' traditional equitable authority absent clear intent otherwise.
Statutory enumerations marked as illustrative or nonexclusive, including by an open-ended residual phrase, do not restrict the broader category to the listed items.
A statutory grant of governmental or agency authority is limited to the powers the statute confers; courts should not imply additional powers beyond the grant.
When interpreting a statute, analogies to other statutes may be useful, but they must be drawn carefully, considering the differences between the statutory schemes.
When a statute uses different words, courts may (where context supports it) presume the terms have different meanings so as to give each independent effect and avoid redundancy.

A modifier should be understood to modify the word or phrase to which it is grammatically attached, and courts should not effectively rearrange the statutory language to attach the modifier elsewhere.
Statutory exemptions from taxation are construed narrowly rather than expansively.
Congressional silence or inaction should not be interpreted as acquiescence to a particular statutory interpretation.
Jurisdictional statutes should be construed narrowly or circumspectly.

When a statute provides that it applies “notwithstanding” another statute, the “notwithstanding” clause indicates that the provision operates despite, and thus overrides, the contrary or otherwise-applicable rule in the referenced statute.
A statute should not be read to withdraw or restrict a court’s jurisdiction (or other previously conferred judicial power) unless Congress clearly indicates that intent.
Courts may not use equitable discretion to rewrite or override statutory rules enacted by Congress.
Under the rule of the last antecedent, a limiting or modifying phrase ordinarily modifies the nearest reasonable antecedent term, not earlier terms in the sentence.
Absent a clear indication that Congress intended strict liability, courts should interpret criminal statutes to include mens rea requirements.
Statutory modifiers should be given operative effect; courts should not read limiting words (e.g., “substantially”) out of the statute or treat them as having no independent force.
Absent a plain indication to the contrary, presume that Congress did not intend a federal statute’s meaning or application to depend on state law.
An express statutory exemption from a provision’s coverage generally implies that the exempted matter would otherwise fall within the provision’s scope or the relevant definitional category.
A statute's failure to address a particular situation, standing alone, is not decisive evidence of Congress's intent.
Courts should read statutory language in light of ordinary English usage, including grammatical structure, but the significance of grammatical cues depends on context.

When Congress enacts a precisely drawn, detailed statutory remedy—especially to fill a perceived gap or replace problematic prior remedies—that specific remedy is generally treated as exclusive and displaces more general remedial or jurisdictional avenues that would otherwise be available.
When a statute grants a right or benefit, it may also imply necessary ancillary rights or procedural incidents needed to make the express right effective.

Statutory grants of public property, franchises, or privileges are construed strictly in favor of the public; only what is clearly and explicitly granted passes, and nothing is granted by implication.
Courts should interpret relevant law to avoid deciding difficult constitutional questions unnecessarily, and should prefer a nonconstitutional ground of decision when available.
Interpretive canons are presumptive guides and may be overcome when the statutory or regulatory text indicates a contrary meaning.
Courts should not assume that a word carries the same meaning in every setting; the same word may carry different meanings in different context.
Courts may not add to, subtract from, or otherwise reconfigure the textual elements of a federal criminal statute.
When a statute (or code) speaks to an issue and departs from the common-law rule, courts are governed by the statute and apply it to the extent it displaces the common law.
A party seeking to take advantage of a statutory exception or exemption bears the burden of establishing that the exception or exemption applies.
Referential terms in a statute (such as “such,” “said,” or “the foregoing”) are ordinarily construed to refer back to the specific antecedent identified by the statutory text.
Courts generally should not rely on a single legislator's floor statement to infer the legislature's collective intent or the meaning of a statute.
Courts may depart from the literal meaning of statutory text only when applying the words as written could not conceivably have been intended; perceived anomalies alone are insufficient.
Criminal statutes should be construed narrowly (strictly) so that courts do not extend criminal liability beyond what Congress has clearly prescribed.

When a federal statute creates a cause of action but supplies no statute of limitations, courts fill the gap by borrowing the most analogous limitations period—often from state law (though sometimes from an analogous federal statute).
A statute's general command is limited by its express exceptions or conditions.
When a statute is enacted to codify existing law, it should be interpreted in light of the preexisting legal principles and practices that Congress sought to codify.
When interpreting a statute, courts should not assume that Congress intended to incorporate technical meanings from specialized fields unless there is evidence of such intent.
When a statute imposes a timing requirement but does not specify a consequence for noncompliance, courts ordinarily should not infer and impose their own coercive sanction for missing the deadline.

In interpreting statutory terms, courts may consult broader legal usage—including other statutes, regulations, and contemporaneous judicial usage—as evidence of the term’s attested semantic range (including whether a particular usage was recognized at the time of enactment), even if that usage is not the most typical one.
Statutes should be construed to give effect to the legislature’s intent, which is the primary object of statutory interpretation.

When a clerical or drafting mistake is evident from context and ordinary grammar, a court may treat it as a scrivener’s error and read the relevant text (including legislative materials, where applicable) to reflect the intended wording.
When a statute incorporates external law by reference and ties that reference to a specified time, the incorporated law is taken as it existed at that time (a static incorporation).
When a statute does not draw a distinction between categories or situations, courts should not imply or create that distinction in interpretation.

When a statute has been amended, interpretation must begin with the amended (current) statutory text and structure; prior interpretive observations about a superseded version remain relevant only to the extent the amendment did not alter the textual or structural features (or other considerations) on which those observations relied.

When a statute authorizes courts to grant equitable relief in general terms, it should be read to invoke only traditional equitable powers and limits unless Congress clearly indicates a departure from them.

When Congress directs courts to use state law to fill gaps in a federal statutory scheme, courts should apply the pertinent state rules to supply the missing content, but only insofar as those state rules are not inconsistent with federal law.
When a statute codifies a common-law doctrine, it should be interpreted in light of that doctrine's preexisting scope and incidents.

Statutes (and regulations) authorizing monetary penalties should be construed to require clear notice; courts should not adopt expansive interpretations of ambiguous provisions to impose penalties where regulated parties lacked fair warning.
No rule of construction requires a penal statute to be strained and distorted to exclude conduct that is clearly intended to be within its scope.
Government practice or past departures from a statute do not change the statute’s legal requirements or create authority that the statute forbids.
When legislative history is ambiguous or unclear, it should not be used to infer a specific congressional intent on an issue.

In determining whether a payment is a “tax” for bankruptcy purposes, courts look to the payment’s operative characteristics—e.g., whether it is an involuntary, state-compelled exaction generally applicable to similarly situated persons or firms—rather than to the label attached to it; nomenclature alone does not control classification.
Courts should interpret a regulation to harmonize it with the controlling statutory language.
A statute should be construed, if fairly possible, to avoid violating international law (the law of nations).
General statutory terms—even words with an expansive ordinary meaning—must be interpreted in their statutory context and may carry implied limitations on their scope.

When interpreting a federal statute that uses an undefined term, courts apply the Dictionary Act’s definition unless the statute’s context indicates that the Dictionary Act definition should not apply.
When a series of terms is followed by a general modifying expression that is equally applicable to each term in the series, the modifier applies to all the terms rather than only to the last one.
When Congress provides a specific, exclusive procedure and forum for judicial review and bars review elsewhere, courts should treat that route as exclusive.
A limitations period that runs from when a claim “accrues” ordinarily begins when the plaintiff has a complete and present cause of action unless the statute provides otherwise.

Courts should not attribute an overarching statutory purpose without a legitimate basis in the statute’s accepted interpretive materials; purpose assertions cannot rest solely on their usefulness in achieving a desired outcome.

Intervening jurisdiction-conferring or jurisdiction-stripping statutes often may be applied to pending cases without triggering the presumption against retroactivity because they usually change only the tribunal (not substantive rights); but such statutes do not automatically apply to pending cases, and ordinary contextual indicators (including negative-implication reasoning) may show Congress intended otherwise.
Punctuation is a minor and noncontrolling aid to statutory interpretation; courts may disregard or repunctuate statutory text when necessary to effect the statute’s purpose and true meaning.

A longstanding, consistent agency interpretation of a statute or regulation—or long agency acquiescence in a regulated industry practice—may be treated as a reason to discount a later, inconsistent agency interpretation.
Statutory time bars are presumptively (but rebuttably) subject to equitable tolling, including in suits against the government.

Courts have final authority to decide pure questions of statutory construction and to mark the bounds of permissible agency interpretation; agencies receive deference only within the scope of authority Congress has delegated to them to fill statutory gaps or make policy choices reasonably.

For statutes granting federal-question jurisdiction over cases “arising under” federal law, a case does not “arise under” federal law unless the federal issue appears on the face of the plaintiff’s well-pleaded complaint; an anticipated federal defense is insufficient.
Courts should not interpret a statute to abrogate or displace a court's traditional or customary powers absent a clear expression of congressional intent.

When a statute contains an express severability clause, courts should follow that textual instruction by severing invalid provisions or applications while leaving the remainder of the statute in force.

Statutory language conferring decisionmaking “judgment” or discretion on an official does not authorize disregard of the statute’s text; it directs the official to exercise discretion only within the statute’s defined limits.
A statute should be construed to abrogate State sovereign immunity only if Congress's intent to do so is stated in unmistakably clear statutory language.
Statutory verb tense (e.g., past vs. present) can indicate the temporal focus and scope of a statutory command, and courts may infer meaning from that grammatical choice.
Courts should not infer statutory intent from silence in the legislative history.
Because “person” in ordinary usage does not include the sovereign, statutory references to a “person” are ordinarily construed not to include the sovereign unless the statute indicates otherwise.
Limitations periods are presumed not to bind the sovereign absent clear legislative intent; limitations that do apply are construed narrowly in the sovereign’s favor.

Courts should apply Chevron (binding) deference to an agency's interpretation only when Congress has delegated to the agency authority to act with the force of law (e.g., through rulemaking or adjudication).
Dictionary definitions do not by themselves determine statutory meaning; ordinary usage and statutory context govern.

A generally applicable default rule (such as Rule 54(d)(1)’s presumption of costs) remains operative unless another provision affirmatively “provides otherwise”—i.e., clearly supplies a contrary directive displacing the default.

Courts generally apply the law in effect at the time they decide a case (including statutes enacted during litigation), unless doing so would cause “manifest injustice” or Congress has indicated (expressly or by clear implication) that the new law should not apply to pending cases.

A statute will not be construed to surrender or contract away a sovereign power (such as the power to tax) unless the surrender is stated in clear, unmistakable terms; ambiguities about such a surrender are resolved in favor of the sovereign.
When a legal text grants authority to do a greater act, it ordinarily encompasses authority to do lesser included acts.
The State is not liable for interest on debts unless there is an express statutory provision or contract that obligates the State to pay such interest.
Courts should not interpret statutes in a way that leads to manifest injustice, in the absence of a clear indication to that effect.
When a treaty and a federal statute conflict, the later-in-time enactment controls in domestic law.
When precedent directs that a statute be liberally construed, courts should give its terms a broad reading consistent with text, context, history, and purposes.
A statute should not be read to incorporate external rules or provisions unless the statute’s text indicates that such incorporation occurs.
Absent a clear statutory or contractual provision to the contrary, courts presume each litigant bears its own attorneys’ fees (the American Rule).
Courts generally should reject a proposed reading that would give statutory words a highly counterintuitive or unorthodox meaning.
Constitutional saving does not authorize courts to rewrite the statute.

A statute’s structure—especially a comprehensive statutory scheme—may be used to infer legislative intent and to determine whether the Legislature meant the statutory scheme to be exclusive (precluding alternative doctrines or defenses not provided for in the scheme).
Although courts should avoid constructions that render statutory language superfluous, a statute is not rendered superfluous merely because it overlaps in some applications with other statutes.
Courts should not construe a statute to impair contracts or disturb vested rights when the statutory language is susceptible of a different construction that avoids that result.
Courts should not infer substantive authorization or delegation merely from legislative silence.
Legislative history cannot be used to cure, supplement, or override deficiencies in the enacted statutory text.
Courts should interpret a jurisdiction-stripping provision in light of the problem it aimed to address and not extend it to materially different suits.
When a legislature expressly repeals specific statutory provisions, unrepealed provisions generally remain in force; an express repeal is limited to what it specifies.
Subsequent legislation is an unreliable basis for inferring the intent or meaning of an earlier statute.

Some statutory procedural requirements are construed as directory rather than mandatory; noncompliance does not necessarily invalidate the underlying action or authority when the requirement is ministerial or intended for administrative/security purposes rather than as a condition precedent.
Under the major questions doctrine, Congress is expected to speak clearly when delegating authority to make decisions of vast economic and political significance.

When a statute provides that a matter is to proceed “in the same manner,” “under the same regulations,” or with “the same effect” as another procedure, those phrases may incorporate aspects of the referenced procedure’s settled rules and limitations, but only to the extent consistent with the statutory context and scheme; they should not be read to import the referenced procedure wholesale where a literal incorporation would be inapplicable or produce contradictions.
When Congress includes a construction clause directing that statutory provisions be construed broadly (or narrowly), courts should apply that direction within the statute’s and Constitution’s limits.
When a statute provides a specific provision for punishment, it is presumed that Congress did not intend to apply additional penalties from prior laws unless clearly stated.
In construing a statute, provisions or consequences that are clearly implied carry the same legal effect as those expressly stated.
A statute's limited scope of application can indicate that it does not reflect a general policy beyond the situations it expressly covers.

When a statute prescribes a particular inquiry, courts should be disciplined by the statute and not interpret based on "freewheeling policy concerns" or graft onto it doctrinal factors from other legal regimes.
Courts should interpret declaratory provisions in statutes not to confer new rights or powers.

When Congress enacts a later statute that unambiguously conflicts with an earlier judicial decision, courts must follow the statute, which supersedes the prior precedent to the extent of the inconsistency.

When Congress enacts a specific amendment to a particular provision despite the existence of a more general provision that might be thought to address the same subject, that action can support an inference that Congress did not understand the general provision to already cover the matter; otherwise the specific amendment would have been unnecessary (especially in construing penalties, which are not extended by implication).

A repeal of a statute is not construed to disturb or divest vested (accrued) rights that were acquired under the statute before its repeal; as to those rights, the prior law is treated as continuing in force.
Courts should interpret criminal statutes so that distinct statutory elements retain independent operative effect and no offense is collapsed into another.
The fact that two statutory provisions overlap in coverage does not by itself justify reading one as implicitly limiting, narrowing, or repealing the other.
When Congress uses different language in related or analogous statutory provisions, courts should assess the context before inferring that Congress intended a difference in meaning or scope.

When a statute directs that X be treated “as” Y for specified statutory purposes (and to any stated extent), interpreters should apply to X the legal consequences and requirements that attach to Y insofar as they are relevant to those purposes and extent, absent a contrary statutory indication.

A federal statute’s saving clause should not be construed to preserve a common-law right or other rule whose continued operation would be absolutely inconsistent with the statute’s provisions or would stand as an obstacle to accomplishing the statute’s objectives; a saving clause cannot be read so that the statute would “destroy itself.”

Statutory silence should not automatically be treated as ambiguity or an implicit delegation of policymaking discretion; when Congress has expressly addressed a matter elsewhere in the statutory scheme, its silence in the provision at issue—considered in light of statutory structure and legislative history—may indicate Congress meant to withhold (and even prohibit) the asserted authority.
The defect or problem in prior law that prompted a statute may inform the intended scope of the statutory change.
Broad statutory language reaches unlisted instances within its terms; omission of a particular example does not itself exclude it from the general category.
When Congress has explicitly mandated pre-emption in the text of a federal enactment, the pre-emption inquiry is straightforward and turns on that express directive.

When Congress expressly prescribes the time limit for enforcing a statutory right, courts must apply that legislated limit as the governing baseline; equitable doctrines may operate only to the extent Congress has not indicated a contrary intent (and courts should not displace the statutory deadline with a different judge-made time bar or extension absent such authorization).

A judicial construction of one statute (or one statute’s provision) should not be treated as controlling the meaning of a different statute absent a sound basis grounded in the latter statute’s text and context.

Where Congress uses particular language and omits readily available alternative wording that would convey a different standard, courts should give effect to Congress’s chosen formulation rather than treating it as if the omitted alternative were enacted.
A statute should not be construed to require the doing of a useless or futile act.

Absent a clear indication from Congress, statutes—especially in penal or forfeiture contexts—should not be construed to abrogate long-established procedural safeguards or entrenched background presumptions.
Ambiguous statutes should be interpreted to avoid unreasonable interference with the sovereign authority of other nations.
A longstanding, consistent construction of a statute in judicial practice (including in lower courts) may be considered as contextual evidence of the statute's meaning.
Statutes should not be construed to permit evasion or circumvention of statutory limits on an actor's (especially an agency's) authority.
Absent clear direction to the contrary from Congress, a federal statute that provides a private right of action is presumed to authorize all appropriate relief, including compensatory damages.
Tax statutes should be construed narrowly: ambiguities or doubts about the scope and meaning of a tax statute should be resolved in favor of the taxpayer.

Courts generally should not interpret a statute on the premise that the legislature misunderstood basic legal context or drafted by mistake; absent contextual indications to the contrary, courts presume the legislature knew the legal framework in which the statute would operate.
Courts should not infer specific procedural mechanisms or compliance approaches from statutory or regulatory silence.
Absent a clear contrary directive, a statute should be construed (where fairly possible) to avoid a construction that would render it unconstitutional.
Some redundancy in statutory language may be contemplated by Congress and does not necessarily justify departing from the text’s natural reading.
The placement of words or phrases within a statute can indicate the scope or applicability of those words or phrases.
Parties cannot, by stipulation, override, rewrite, or negate what a statute provides.

A statutory definition does not necessarily govern every occurrence of the defined term throughout a statute; its applicability may be limited by the statute’s structure or by the particular provisions in which the term appears.

When a penal statute is repealed or expires, enforcement of penalties and continuation of prosecutions for prior violations cease unless a saving provision preserves liability or authorizes continued proceedings.
Congressional silence—especially where extended legislative deliberations would be expected to address the issue—may be probative evidence of statutory meaning (a negative inference from silence).
Courts generally presume that statutes do not concern themselves with trifles (de minimis matters), absent a clear indication to the contrary.
Courts generally should not read appropriations legislation (or similar funding measures) as modifying or amending substantive law absent a clear indication that Congress meant to do so.
Courts may draw interpretive inferences from statutory grammar such as Congress's use of the singular versus the plural.

Questions of pre-emption (including conflict pre-emption) should be resolved by reference to enacted federal statutory text and duly authorized regulations (and what is set forth in, or necessarily follows from, that text), not by extra-textual notions of purpose or policy that Congress did not express and that are not plainly inferable from what it enacted.
Courts should avoid rigid literalism
When a statute uses two terms or phrases interchangeably in context, that usage suggests (but does not conclusively establish) that the legislature intended them to have the same meaning.

When Congress enacts or revises federal criminal statutes without addressing an issue (e.g., an affirmative defense or burden of proof), courts presume Congress legislated against the backdrop of settled Anglo-American judicial/common-law understandings (as reflected in precedent and related legal sources such as treatises and the Model Penal Code) and apply those background principles unless the statute indicates a contrary intent.

When a statute leaves courts discretion to adopt procedures or remedies, that discretion (and any resulting solution) must be exercised in a manner compatible with the statute’s purposes and not in a way that would undermine them.

When a statute prohibits an act or imposes a penalty for its commission, courts should examine the statute as a whole to determine whether the legislature intended also to render unenforceable (or void) contracts made in contravention of the statute; illegality or a penalty alone does not automatically avoid such contracts.
Forfeitures should not be inferred from doubtful or ambiguous statutory language; clear language is required to impose a forfeiture.

Courts should be hesitant to construe a federal criminal statute to federalize ordinary crimes traditionally prosecuted by the States unless the statute clearly indicates that Congress intended such a broad reach.

When determining whether Congress authorized cumulative punishments for two offenses, apply the Blockburger same-elements test: presume the offenses are distinct (and cumulative punishments permissible) if each requires proof of an element the other does not, absent a clear indication of contrary legislative intent.

When Congress creates a statutory cause of action that resembles a common-law claim, courts presume Congress incorporated the common-law background rules and elements absent express statutory language to the contrary.

When a statute’s application turns on whether a prior conviction is for a specified type of offense, courts determine the match by reference to the offense’s legal definition (its elements), not the defendant’s actual conduct in the prior case.
Absent contrary indication, statutory phrases that denote causation (e.g., “because of,” “based on,” “by reason of,” “as a result of”) are ordinarily read to require but-for causation.

When a statute specifies particular legal consequences or remedies for a violation, courts generally should not infer additional statutory consequences (such as voidness) beyond those the statute provides.

A term may be interpreted in light of surrounding terms (noscitur a sociis)—especially when a genuine list or string of terms suggests a common attribute—so that the grouped words are given related meaning; but the canon does not apply where there is no meaningful set of associated terms from which to extrapolate, and an example or narrow companion term does not automatically narrow a broader term.

Broad or general statutory terms (such as “any person”) need not be applied at their maximum literal scope; instead, they must be read as limited to cases within the enacting sovereign’s jurisdiction and to the objects the legislature intended to reach.

Courts generally should not find field pre-emption absent express statutory language or other strong indicia (e.g., a pervasive federal regulatory scheme) showing Congress intended to occupy the field.

When the Court’s precedents impose a clear-statement requirement for a particular legal consequence, that requirement must be satisfied by a clear statement from the legislature in enacted law (not by legislative history or other non-enacted materials such as Advisory Committee Notes).

Statutory provisions should be read in context, including by considering how related clauses interact; however, contextual inferences (including redundancy/superfluity concerns) ordinarily cannot overcome the plain language of an otherwise clear provision.
Absent clear indication, statutes should not be construed to create an implausible regulatory or remedial vacuum.
A legal document, including a statute, is presumed to take effect on the date it bears.

To determine whether repeated conduct constitutes multiple offenses or a single continuing offense under a statute, ask whether the statute prohibits discrete individual acts (making each act separately punishable) or instead targets a continuous course of conduct (yielding only one punishable offense).

When a statute enacts or prohibits conduct for the especial benefit of a person or class, and a violation injures a member of that benefited class, a right to a remedy— including recovery of damages from the party in default—may be implied under the statute.
A statutory term’s meaning or referent can be informed by how the statute itself uses that term.

When a statute authorizes a federal agency or government instrumentality to “sue and be sued,” it is presumed to have fully waived immunity; that presumption is overcome only if, as to particular types of suits, there is clearly contrary legislative intent.

If Congress has expressly prescribed a statute’s temporal reach (i.e., its proper reach as applied to pre-enactment events), courts must follow that express instruction and need not resort to judicial default rules or presumptions (such as the presumption against retroactivity).
A statutory designation of the forum for a procedural step ordinarily excludes other fora for that step.
When a statute is repealed, it is treated as though it had never been enacted, and surviving sections must be construed without regard to the repealed statute.

When a statute or treaty does not address a claimed legal effect or enforcement mechanism—especially where its text is best read as conferring only jurisdiction—courts should be reluctant to infer that effect or mechanism from silence, and should not treat the instrument as creating such obligations absent textual support (or implementing legislation where required).
When interpreting statutes enacted for the benefit of Indians or tribes, ambiguities are construed in favor of the Indians or tribes.

When statutory text uses a term of art, it is generally presumed to carry its specialized meaning and to remain stable across contexts; but where a different statutory purpose or context indicates otherwise, the term may take on a different meaning. In the absence of a conflicting purpose or context, usage/definitions in other statutes may be evidence of Congress’s understanding of the term.

A judgment or order qualifies as "final" for purposes of a statute when it conclusively resolves all issues in the case and leaves nothing for the lower court to do except perform ministerial acts (such as entering the judgment).
When a statutory condition is tied to a specified time, compliance is determined as of that time rather than by subsequent events.

Unless the statutory text indicates otherwise, the mens rea term “knowingly” requires proof that the defendant knew the facts that constitute the offense (not necessarily that the defendant knew the conduct was unlawful).
Congress is presumed to legislate with awareness of established industry practices and background conditions in the regulated field.
Courts require a clear statement before construing a statute to deny any judicial forum for a colorable constitutional claim.

In assessing a statute’s temporal reach under the presumption against retroactivity, applying a new statute to post-effective-date continuation of ongoing unlawful conduct (an “indefinitely continuing violation”) is treated as prospective—especially where the statute’s predicate is the continued conduct and the regulated party can end the violation—though the application may look back to an earlier act that began the violation.

Where a statutory command is expressly conditional—especially when it turns on an official’s discretionary determination (e.g., “shall do X if the Secretary decides Y”)—the statute should not be read as an unconditional, self-executing mandate; the condition limits when (and whether) the duty or prohibition comes into being.
There is a general presumption that the mens rea specified in a criminal statute applies to all elements of the offense, unless context indicates otherwise.

Statutory language should be interpreted in a contextual, purpose-consistent way rather than through rigid, mechanical application of a single numerical or formal metric when the statute’s standard calls for consideration of circumstances.
Courts should not force a common-law or other term-of-art meaning onto a statutory context in which it does not fit.
When interpreting a tax statute, courts should consider the actual operation and effect of the statute, not just what the statute on its face purports to do.
A court generally does not grant Chevron deference to an agency’s interpretation of a statute the agency is not charged with administering.

Statutes of limitations applicable to suits for debts or money demands generally run only against the judicial remedy (the right to bring suit) and do not, by themselves, discharge the debt or extinguish (or even impair) the underlying right or obligation; accordingly, the creditor may use other lawful means of collection unless the statute clearly provides otherwise.

A statutory phrase may operate as a term of art whose meaning is established by the statute’s definitional/contextual usage; when the statutory scheme shows such a specialized meaning, courts should apply that meaning rather than ordinary usage.

Statutory provisions that specify the method of collecting or enforcing an existing duty are construed as remedial—altering the remedy or means of enforcement—rather than as creating or increasing the underlying substantive obligation, absent a statutory indication that a new obligation is being imposed.
Subsequent legislative action (such as amendments or extensions) is a weak basis for inferring congressional ratification of an administrative interpretation.
Practical difficulties, expense, or administrability concerns do not justify departing from or creating exceptions to the requirements imposed by a statute’s terms.

When a statute provides a particular remedy or enforcement method, courts should not presume that remedy is exclusive—or that it displaces the Government’s well-recognized existing enforcement mechanisms—unless the statute’s text clearly and specifically indicates Congress’s intent to do so.
When a statute requires computation of time from an act or event, the day on which the act or event occurs is included in the computation.
When the text of the United States Code conflicts with the text of the Statutes at Large, the Statutes at Large (the enacted law) control.
When a statute provides that a fact or finding is "prima facie evidence" of another fact, it establishes a rebuttable presumption rather than conclusive proof.

A saving clause is generally construed to preserve the continued operation of preexisting law, not to create or require new causes of action or new enforcement mechanisms for rights newly created by the statute.

When a statute directs a decisionmaker to "consider" certain factors, it requires genuine consideration of all relevant/required factors but does not by itself dictate any particular outcome or make any single factor automatically dispositive.

An agency’s interpretation advanced solely as a litigating position, and not grounded in regulations, rulings, or consistent administrative practice, should receive less weight from a court when interpreting the law.

In determining whether a federal statute’s pre-emption (or similar coverage) provision reaches a state measure, courts should look to the measure’s practical effect and operation, not merely its formal source or label (e.g., common law versus statute or regulation).

When Congress has clearly drawn a jurisdictional or remedial line between categories (e.g., contract claims versus tort claims), courts should not “fritter away” that distinction by recharacterizing claims so as to evade the statutory limit.

When a statute uses narrower, limiting language (e.g., "joinder" of the United States as a "necessary party") rather than the broader formulations used in other statutes (e.g., authorizing "any claim against the United States"), the contrast supports giving effect to the limitation and reading the statute to authorize only the narrower category—especially where the provision is asserted as a waiver of sovereign immunity, which is strictly construed.

When interpreting a statute, the canon against superfluity is useful only if there is a competing interpretation that gives effect to every clause and word (i.e., avoids treating any statutory language as surplusage).
Uncertain or inconsistent administrative practice carries little interpretive weight and does not support a contrary statutory interpretation.
Legislative authorization to exercise the takings power should be found only when the statute contains an express provision or the authorization arises by necessary implication.

A prior judicial construction forecloses (and thus prevails over) a later agency interpretation otherwise eligible for Chevron deference only when the prior court held the statute’s meaning was unambiguous, leaving no room for agency interpretive discretion.
A statute that imposes a penalty for an act does not, by implication, authorize the act to be done.
Courts do not defer to the Department of Justice's interpretation of criminal laws that it prosecutes.
Courts should give narrow dimensions to any judicially-created implied private right of action.

When Congress expressly addresses a principle or standard in one statutory provision, courts should not infer that Congress silently authorized a contrary departure from that principle in another provision without clear textual indication.

Courts, applying the traditional tools of statutory construction, ordinarily expect Congress to speak clearly if it intends to exempt an entire subject area or particular provisions from an agency’s generally conferred rulemaking/interpretive authority; absent clear language, courts are reluctant to infer such a carve-out.
General legislative history statements should not be used to interpret specific statutory provisions unless they directly address the provision in question.
If a statutory rule applies (or a conclusion follows) in a given case, it applies with even greater force in a stronger case (a fortiori reasoning).

Statutory language should be construed in light of the specialized legal principles and background concepts of the field the statute addresses, where those principles inform how the statutory terms operate in practice.
Statutory terms should not be given an unduly narrow construction when the text, read fairly in context, supports a broader application.
The enactment of a new statute does not necessarily imply that the subject matter was not covered by previous statutes.

When interpreting a statutorily created cause of action, courts presume that it extends only to plaintiffs whose interests fall within the zone of interests protected by the statute. Congress is presumed to legislate against this background limitation (often described as applying unless expressly negated), though it may be more accurate to say the limitation always applies and particular statutes may simply protect an unusually expansive range of interests.

When Congress has addressed a subject explicitly in specific provisions (especially as part of a comprehensive scheme), courts should not ordinarily read a separate, more general provision that omits any reference to that subject as covering it by implication—particularly where doing so would defeat an express repeal or expand a penal statute beyond its text.
Simultaneous repeal and substantially similar reenactment ordinarily continue the prior law and its legal operation without interruption.

When a statute requires a department head (e.g., a Secretary) to give notice or perform an official act, it ordinarily permits performance through authorized subordinates acting under the official’s sanction and direction, absent clear statutory language requiring personal action; courts should not read such provisions to demand the officer personally sign or transmit every communication where that would be impracticable.
When a statute’s text has a plain (ordinary) meaning that encompasses a concept, courts should not treat Congress’s failure to use a particular phrase or label for that concept as dispositive.

When a statutory right is conditioned on the lawful performance of required official or legally prescribed acts, and the record does not affirmatively show noncompliance, courts presume that those acts were properly performed in accordance with law (presumption of regularity / omnia praesumuntur rite esse acta).

When reviewing an agency’s interpretation of a statute, courts often apply Chevron’s two-step framework: they first ask whether the statute is ambiguous (i.e., whether Congress has spoken clearly to the issue), and if it is, they then ask whether the agency’s interpretation is reasonable and defer to it. But in extraordinary cases involving questions of deep economic and political significance, a court may decline to find implicit delegation and instead determine the statute’s best reading itself.
A court should not adopt a construction that misconstrues one statutory provision in order to restore or improve the operation of another provision to serve a perceived statutory function or policy.

When a statute incorporates an earlier statute by reference, repeal of the earlier (incorporated) statute does not repeal the later (incorporating) statute; the later statute remains in force unless it is repealed expressly or by necessary implication (not by mere possibility or inference).
A provision’s placement within a statutory code or compilation is not, by itself, dispositive of its meaning or legal character.

Courts may interpret a statute to preempt state law when the statute evinces a clear and manifest congressional purpose, including factors such as a pervasive federal regulatory scheme, a dominant federal interest, or conflict between state law and federal objectives.

Where a statute prescribes procedural steps, a merely technical or non-prejudicial deviation that still accomplishes the statute’s essential requirement (i.e., is in effect a compliance) does not, by itself, invalidate the proceeding or defeat the court’s jurisdiction—especially on collateral attack.

A § 1983 cause of action is generally and presumptively available to remedy violations of federal law unless the federal statute at issue is part of a statutory scheme that is clearly incompatible with (and thus implicitly precludes) enforcement through § 1983.

Absent some other indication in the statutory text or context, a statutory reference to a State’s “requirements” in a federal express pre-emption provision should be construed to include the State’s common-law duties.
Interpreters should apply traditional interpretive tools and give effect to a statute’s clear text before concluding that the statute is ambiguous.

General statutory review provisions are ordinarily construed to permit review only of agency rulings or orders that are final in character; preliminary or preparatory determinations (including status determinations made in preparation for later action) are not reviewable under such general review provisions unless the determination has an immediate, effectively final operative effect.

Courts should be wary of construing a statute so broadly that it would effectively modify or add conditions to other statutes’ specific, categorical mandates for federal agencies across the U.S. Code absent clear congressional direction.
Courts should not apply interpretive rules mechanically when doing so would require accepting unlikely or unreasonable premises about statutory meaning.

When a statute creates a cause of action or assigns a matter to a court but does not prescribe special procedures, courts apply the usual procedures and adjudicate according to the evidence and the applicable law.

Language authorizing judicial review of a 'final order' is construed to authorize review of all matters on which the validity of the final order is contingent, not just those determinations made at the hearing.

When a statute requires a description or designation, compliance does not ordinarily depend on the use of particular formulaic words if the substance of the required information is adequately conveyed.

When Congress regulates the amount or conditions of a remedy (e.g., salvage), that regulation may indicate Congress assumed and recognized the existence or lawfulness of the underlying right/authority (e.g., a right to recapture or claim salvage) even if Congress did not confer that right in express terms.

When a federal court borrows a state statute of limitations for a federal claim because federal law supplies no limitations period, it also borrows the state’s coordinate tolling rules—unless applying those state tolling rules would be inconsistent with the Constitution or federal law/policy.

When a statute confers decisionmaking authority in terms so discretionary that it supplies no meaningful standard for a court to apply, the statute is ordinarily read to preclude judicial review of that decision.

A statute’s general words should not be presumed to apply to the sovereign, but that presumption is weaker as to government agents and may be overcome when the statute’s general words are aimed at preventing injury or wrongdoing.

When a statute authorizes an administrative officer to determine questions of fact, courts should treat those factual determinations as binding, except where the officer exceeds statutory authority—such as by acting arbitrarily or capriciously, without evidentiary support, or through procedures lacking basic fairness and reasonableness.
A statute is not ambiguous (and may still have a plain/natural meaning) merely because judges or courts have disagreed about its interpretation.
Remedial or enforcement provisions do not, without clear text, alter a statute’s independently imposed substantive duties.
Statutory language that appears permissive (e.g., that an officer is “authorized” to act) may be construed as mandatory where the statute concerns a public duty or matter of public concern.
A statutory right may be waived or relinquished unless the statute forbids waiver or otherwise indicates the right is nonwaivable.

When a statute creates a new cause of action (or liability) and in the same enactment specifies a time within which suit must be brought, the time limit is construed as a limitation on the statutory right/liability itself rather than a mere procedural limit on the remedy.
Administrative interpretations of other statutes do not control the interpretation of the statute at issue, though they may be considered as potentially persuasive or contextual evidence.

As a general rule, the law disregards fractions of a day when determining the timing/effect of legal acts, but that convenience rule yields and courts will consider the precise time of day when necessary to serve justice or resolve conflicting rights/interests.

Broad “public interest” delegations in an agency statute are construed in light of the statute’s scheme and the agency’s traditional/regulatory subject-matter domain, and do not confer a general license to pursue the public welfare at large.

Context-dependent statutory terms (e.g., “appropriate” and “necessary”) must be interpreted in light of their surrounding statutory context, including the term’s place and function within the broader statutory/regulatory scheme; giving such terms content requires attention to those surrounding circumstances.
When a repealing statute is itself repealed, the earlier statute is not revived by implication; revival occurs only if the legislature expressly provides for it.

Courts should not treat identification (or joinder) of an additional liable party as a prerequisite to a statutory cause of action unless the statute makes that identification indispensable to making out the claim; where the statute authorizes recovery against the primary defendant even if the additional party cannot be identified, failure to identify that party does not defeat the claim.

Federal installations are subject to state regulation only when, and only to the extent that, Congress has clearly and unambiguously authorized such regulation (i.e., waivers of federal immunity from state regulation are not implied absent a clear statement).

General statutory grants of public lands are read as subject to an implied exception for lands that, at the time of enactment, had already been withdrawn from the public domain by federal reservation, absent clear contrary congressional intent.

If a statute authorizes an application or proceeding but provides no deadline, courts may construe the statute to require that the right be exercised within a reasonable time, assessed under the circumstances.

If statutory text is ambiguous or inconclusive on the question presented, a court may consult other interpretive sources—including relevant pre-enactment case law, especially where the statute was intended to codify existing doctrine—to help determine the statute’s meaning.

In interpreting a statutory cause of action, courts must determine what Congress actually authorized and may not create or curtail the cause of action based on the court’s independent policy judgment.

Interpret the operative legal instrument by reference to its own terms; do not use the terms of a different instrument to override or negate the meaning and scope established by the text being construed (absent incorporation or clear contextual linkage).
Legislative history from one statute should not be transposed to interpret another statute unless there is a compelling indication that Congress intended the same meaning.

Statutes authorizing compensation or fees for public officers are construed to require clear legal authorization; public officers are entitled to compensation only when the law clearly provides for it.
Statutory duties and obligations should not be construed to require unlawful conduct; a person cannot be held to have violated a statutory duty for failing to take an action that would break the law.
Statutory language phrased as a maximum (e.g., “not to exceed”) ordinarily imposes a ceiling but does not establish a floor, leaving discretion below the stated upper limit.
The absence of a specific exclusion in a statute can support an inference that the statute's broad terms apply.

The inclusion of an express preemption provision does not, by negative implication alone, foreclose the possibility that implied conflict preemption may also apply; implied conflict preemption remains available if an actual conflict is shown.
The meaning of the term 'willfully' in a statute is context-dependent and can vary based on the specific legal context in which it is used.
Whether equitable tolling applies to a statutory deadline depends on Congress’s intent as reflected in the statute and its context.

When Congress legislates in the shadow of an existing administrative scheme—especially by conferring remedial and rulemaking authority in terms similar to an earlier delegation—it is reasonable to infer that Congress expected the agency to build on and extend that established framework (including comparable administrative remedies) unless the statute indicates otherwise.

When a statute refers generally to what is permitted or “available by law,” and contains no indication that it is pegged to enactment-era rules, the reference is ordinarily read as ambulatory—incorporating the law as it exists from time to time rather than freezing the law as of the statute’s enactment.

When a civil statute imposes no specific evidentiary burden, courts ordinarily apply the default civil standard—preponderance of the evidence—absent text, context, or precedent justifying a heightened burden.

When a statute conditions jurisdiction on an ‘amount in dispute’ (or ‘amount in controversy’), the amount is determined by the value of the matter actually disputed between the parties, not by contingent, collateral, or consequential losses that may follow from the judgment.
Procedural prerequisites expressly attached to a statutory consequence must be satisfied before that consequence follows.

When a statute is urged to be read to allow the Executive—absent a clear statement from Congress—to remove cases from the Judiciary’s domain (i.e., to strip or preclude judicial review based on executive discretion), separation-of-powers concerns counsel against adopting that interpretation.

When a statute uses purposive language such as requiring that conduct be “designed … to” achieve a result, courts should construe that text to require proof that achieving the result was a purpose of the conduct, not merely that the conduct had that effect.

When applying a statutory rule (especially broad general terms) to a particular circumstance would be inconsistent with the statute’s underlying rationale or purpose—e.g., would produce absurd or unworkable results—courts may construe the rule to contain an implied limitation or exception so it does not govern that circumstance.

Where statutory language contains multiple antecedents and multiple consequents (e.g., several items followed by several verbs, modifiers, or remedial directions), it should be read distributively so that each consequent is applied to its proper corresponding antecedent (*reddenda singula singulis*), rather than applying every term to every item.

When statutory language provides that certain rules apply “until” a specified event occurs, the statute, by its terms, addresses only the pre-event period and cannot be read to supply or imply rules (or affirmative approval) for what happens after the event, absent additional statutory text.

When statutory text assigns a metric or attribute to a specified entity (and uses that entity as the object of the provision), the relevant population/unit for applying that metric must be that entity; an interpretation that reassigns the metric to a different unit (e.g., subunits) without textual indication lacks textual support and should be rejected.

Where a statute is challenged as unconstitutionally vague, it ordinarily should not be deemed facially invalid if it is readily subject to a narrowing construction (often by the state courts); as part of such a narrowing construction, courts may, where the text is reasonably susceptible, read in a scienter (knowledge) requirement to mitigate vagueness/constitutional concerns.

Where a statute’s text and structure specify a sequence of steps, courts may treat that sequencing as indicating the intended order and whether one step is a prerequisite to another (e.g., that a later step need not occur before an earlier-authorized action).

A court may treat a statutory offense as a “public welfare offense” and therefore infer that Congress dispensed with a mens rea requirement (at least as to certain elements) when the statute regulates conduct that a reasonable person would recognize as subject to stringent public regulation and as posing a serious risk to public health or safety—rather than ordinary, apparently innocent conduct.
An intention to abrogate or modify a treaty is not lightly imputed to Congress; clear legislative intent is required.

A public act should not be construed to contemplate or authorize a breach of the government’s pledged public faith unless that construction is unavoidable—i.e., unless no other reasonable construction is possible.

A statute ordinarily should not be construed to effect a major departure from traditional fee-shifting practice (or other settled background norms) unless the text—often reinforced by legislative indicia—clearly signals that change.

A statutory exception (or exemption) to an otherwise applicable statutory requirement is not itself a command to do the opposite; at most it removes that statutory requirement and leaves open whether some other source of law independently imposes the requirement.
A statutory precondition that admits multiple, congressionally authorized exceptions is a contextual indicator against treating the precondition as jurisdictional (though it is not dispositive).
Absent a clear statutory indication to the contrary, a statute should be interpreted as not precluding traditional common-law defenses (such as self-defense).

Absent a statutory (or other legal) prohibition, a claimant’s existing, legally cognizable property/claim rights are presumptively conveyable; courts should not invalidate a conveyance by implying a transfer bar without a clear legal prohibition.

Absent a statutory limitation on the President’s removal authority, an executive officer (particularly an agency head) is generally presumed to be removable at will (to serve at the President’s pleasure).
Congress is presumed to speak in clear (plain) terms when it intends to circumscribe agency discretion, and in capacious terms when it intends to enlarge agency discretion.

If legislation has been enacted in due form, courts generally will not investigate the legislature’s motives or the methods by which the enactment was obtained, and will instead confine review to the enactment’s text and legal effect.

Courts may draw interpretive inferences from Congress’s choice of definite versus indefinite articles (e.g., “the” vs. “a/an”) in statutory text, including about whether a requirement is exclusive or nonexclusive.
When reliable aids to statutory construction are available, courts may use them to determine the meaning of statutory words even if the text appears clear on a superficial reading.
Congress is presumed to legislate with knowledge of established canons and judicial interpretive practices.

Courts should avoid construing a statute in a way that would cause unwarranted judicial interference in the conduct of foreign policy or the delicate field of international relations unless Congress has clearly expressed an affirmative intention to that effect.

Courts should be cautious about inferring that Congress, by reenacting, revising, or recodifying a statute, approved or ratified a prior interpretation; such an inference is especially dubious when it would override statutory text (particularly in criminal statutes) and when the prior interpretation was not a settled judicial or responsible agency construction or was internally inconsistent.
Courts should not allow technical or euphemistic refinements in terminology to generate artificial ambiguities or distinctions that obscure the substantive meaning and operation of a statute.
Courts should not presume that Congress was aware of a judicial decision interpreting a statute unless there is some showing that Congress knew of that interpretation.
Courts should not rely on a statute’s supposed “plain meaning” when the relevant term is reasonably susceptible to more than one plausible interpretation.

Statutory interpretation should not rest on judges’ (or a court’s) preconceived moral or ethical views; in discerning congressional intent, courts should instead look to legitimate indicia such as the statute’s text and (where appropriate) legislative history.

Courts should not treat distinct statutory provisions (including separately enacted provisions creating distinct offenses) as mere relabelings of the same prohibition; unless it can be reasonably maintained that Congress was only giving different labels to the same thing, different provisions are presumed to have independent effect.

In construing a statute of limitations (or similar time bar) with a disability-saving/tolling proviso, the disability must exist at the time the cause of action (or right to sue/appeal) accrues in order to prevent the statute from running; once the limitations period has commenced, a subsequently arising disability does not interrupt it.

Implied repeals of the antitrust laws by a later or specialized regulatory statute are strongly disfavored; a regulatory scheme should not be read to render the generally applicable antitrust laws inapplicable absent clear incompatibility (i.e., “plain repugnancy”) between the antitrust and regulatory provisions (typically where regulation is pervasive and Congress plainly intended to substitute government supervision for competition).
Jurisdiction-conferring statutory elements are ordinarily not read to require the defendant’s knowledge of the jurisdictional fact, unless Congress clearly indicates otherwise.

Related statutory phrases should be construed together—rather than in isolation—especially where that integrated reading supports a narrower, constitutionally unproblematic construction of the statute as a whole (and may obviate the need to consider severability).
When construing statutes or procedural rules affecting entitlement to a jury, courts should resolve doubts in favor of trial by jury in order to protect the constitutional right to a jury trial.

Statutes should, where fairly possible, be construed so that their jurisdictional scope (and other structural provisions) is consistent with—and does not undermine—the statute’s substantive objectives, avoiding a reading that sets the statute’s operative parts at odds with its remedial or substantive aims.
Statutory exceptions should be read fairly, not narrowly.

Statutory provisions making an agency’s determination “final” are construed to presume that the determination was reached through the hearing/procedures the governing law contemplates; finality does not attach where that presupposed good-faith process is absent.

When Congress has enacted a comprehensive statutory/regulatory scheme that addresses the problem at issue, leaving no interstice for federal common law to fill, federal common law is displaced; courts may not create or apply federal common law merely because they disagree with the manner in which the statute or responsible agencies have chosen to address the problem.

When a statute provides no definite legal test and instead states a general requirement, the statute should be implemented through a practical, flexible assessment rather than a rigid, purely legalistic rule.

When a limitations statute (or an amendment) first subjects a cause of action to a limitations period, the period is calculated from the time the cause of action first becomes subject to the statute, unless the legislature specifies a different starting point.

When a statute (such as CERCLA) does not clearly resolve an issue that common-law doctrine traditionally governs (e.g., the scope of liability, including divisibility/apportionment), courts may treat Congress as having left that issue to be determined by traditional and evolving common-law principles (often reflected in sources like the Restatement), unless the statute clearly provides otherwise.

When a statute commits a procedural step (such as appointing experts or holding a hearing) to an official’s or court’s discretion, the statute ordinarily does not create an enforceable right or entitlement to that discretionary procedure absent clear contrary text.

When a statute’s operative text is a translation (or has competing translations), courts may consult the original-language version and compare credible translations to determine the provision’s meaning.

When a statute uses a general category followed by “including” and examples, the examples may be illustrative and can be limited by the scope of the preceding general category, rather than automatically expanding it.
When statutory language refers to conduct in an approving or legitimizing way, it is ordinarily understood to refer to lawful conduct rather than unlawful conduct.

When adjacent, structurally parallel statutory provisions are linked by contrastive language (e.g., “other”), the “other” term is ordinarily read by reference to the immediately preceding provision—covering persons or things other than the specifically listed category in that preceding provision.

When an agency’s statutory power is described as remedial (e.g., authority to order “affirmative action” to effectuate the statute), that grant is construed to permit measures that remedy or undo the effects of the violation, not to confer punitive jurisdiction to impose penalties chosen to punish the violator.

When deciding whether a statute implicitly precludes/displaces another cause of action or remedy, the key inquiry is whether Congress affirmatively intended that preclusion; mere congressional expectations or lack of anticipation are not enough.
