When multiple statutory provisions are expressly governed by the same definitional section, the definitions (and related interpretive rules) should be applied consistently across those provisions, including where the provisions use materially equivalent phrasing.

A cause of action or liability created solely by statute (a “factitious” or “statute” right) ordinarily exists only for the life of the statute that creates it and lapses upon the statute’s expiration or repeal, unless preserved by a saving provision (including a general saving statute).

A severability (saving) clause generally means that if a statutory provision is held invalid, other provisions may remain effective, but the clause does not itself supply a workable severance unless the statute provides an identifiable basis (a “line of severance”) for separating valid from invalid applications.
A statute (especially a fee-shifting provision) should be interpreted in light of the statutory provisions it was designed to effectuate and the statute’s purposes.

A statute should not be given an extravagant or implausibly broad construction—especially one that would attribute extraordinary or unauthorized power to the enacting government—when a narrower, more plausible construction is available.

A statute should not be interpreted as a mere restatement of preexisting law or settled executive practice (e.g., an existing executive order) such that Congress would have had little reason to legislate; courts should prefer a reading under which the enactment meaningfully changes or adds to the prior legal landscape.

A statute will not be construed to abrogate Indian treaty rights unless Congress has clearly and plainly—i.e., unmistakably—expressed its intent to do so (as shown by the statute’s text and/or other clear evidence of legislative purpose).
A statute’s remedial and enforcement provisions may, as contextual evidence, corroborate (but do not independently control) a narrower or broader reading of the statute’s substantive prohibitions.

Absent a congressional provision to the contrary, when Congress has left a matter to state law (e.g., state guardianship proceedings), questions such as compliance with state procedures and the time and mode for seeking correction of state-court errors—including the effect of failing to do so—are controlled by state law.
When a statute authorizes an act to be done up to and including a specified day, and that day falls on Sunday (a dies non), the act may generally be done on the following day.

Absent clear statutory text, a designation or delegation of duties/authority does not transform the designee into the designating official or into a different statutory entity (e.g., does not convert the designee into an “agency”) merely because it performs functions the other entity could perform.
Ambiguities in statutory language should be resolved in a way that does not imperil substantial rights.
Congress's appropriation of funds for a specific purpose can be interpreted as an indirect approval of prior actions taken by the President related to that purpose.

Congressional reenactment of statutory language does not, by itself, permanently entrench an agency’s existing interpretation so as to prevent the agency from changing that interpretation prospectively through authorized rulemaking.

Courts may interpret a statute (including the scope of a preemption clause) in light of the legal landscape at enactment—including existing common-law remedies and regulatory regimes—to infer what Congress meant to alter or preserve; absent a clear indication, Congress is not assumed to have displaced background common-law liability.

Courts should avoid interpreting a damages/remedial provision in a way that would allow a defendant to profit from its own wrong or to retain illegal profits (e.g., by adopting a rule that lets the violator keep unlawful overcharges).

Courts should be wary of interpreting a statute to require federal courts to undertake an endless exercise of second-guessing local governmental programs—especially where the statute does not supply clear, administrable standards for such judicial review.
Delegated powers that curtail or dilute natural activities that may be necessary to citizen well-being, such as travel, should be construed narrowly.

Do not treat liability exposure or other incidental regulatory effects that may induce regulated parties to change conduct as a legal “requirement” or “mandate”; a statutory/state-law “requirement” refers to a rule of law that must be obeyed (leaving no choice for a party wishing to comply), absent clear text to the contrary.

Even where a statute uses language that might be read prospectively (e.g., “shall have been approved”), a confirmatory/curative statute may be construed to ratify and validate prior actions when the statute’s text, purpose, and context show Congress intended to remove existing doubt by confirming what has already occurred.

General statutory language imposing taxation is presumed not to apply to a State’s own property (or that of its municipalities/political subdivisions) unless the legislature clearly expresses an intent to include it.

If a statute imposes duties on an administrative body, courts will provide a judicial remedy for wanton or unlawful disregard of those duties; where the statute does not expressly provide for judicial relief, a remedy in the courts may be implied as necessary to prevent the statutory duty from being unenforceable or unreviewable.

If statutory language plainly resolves the issue, courts give effect to that clear meaning; if the text does not clearly resolve the question presented, courts may consult legislative history to discern Congress’s intent.

In applying Chevron to an agency’s interpretation of an ambiguous statute, courts do not withhold Chevron analysis or deference merely because the agency’s position has been inconsistent, the regulation is not contemporaneous with the statute, or the regulation was prompted by litigation.

Judicial constructions or definitions of statutory terms must be read in their proper context—i.e., in light of the statute and the specific issue decided—rather than applied in isolation as dispositive of different questions.
Statutory chapter headings (and similar headings) do not give rise to an inference or presumption about the statute’s substantive meaning or construction.

Only statutes that are penal in the technical/legal sense (not merely because they impose a penalty or forfeiture) are construed with great strictness in favor of the defendant; remedial statutes enacted to prevent fraud or effect a public good may be construed to best accomplish legislative intent.
Prefatory or introductory statutory language can qualify and limit the scope of an operative clause, and the two should be read together to determine the provision’s reach.

When Congress enacts legislation that can fairly be understood as confirming or incorporating a longstanding judicial doctrine or practice, courts may treat that enactment as evidence of congressional approval (ratification) of the established doctrine or practice.
Committee reports and legislative history cannot impose binding appropriations restrictions absent enacted statutory language.
Statutes creating evidentiary privileges are to be strictly construed, so as to avoid interpretations that unnecessarily exclude otherwise competent evidence.

Statutory language is ordinarily read against settled background principles of government contracting/appropriations law; an interpretation that would depart from those ordinary principles is unlikely absent evidence that Congress intended the departure.

Statutory language need not be read to require that every verb in a phrase sensibly applies to every noun in that phrase; courts need not narrow a statute merely because some verb–noun combinations would be inapt, nor must Congress add phrase-by-phrase exemptions for applications in which part of a phrase is unnecessary.

Statutory provisions directing courts to disregard harmless errors (e.g., 28 U.S.C. § 2111) should be applied in a manner consistent with their purpose of avoiding reversals for mere technicalities; accordingly, harmless-error review should ordinarily be conducted case-specifically on the record, and rigid presumptions or mandatory rules that mechanically require findings of prejudice are disfavored.
The existence of an express administrative enforcement mechanism in a statute does not, by itself, foreclose inferring an implied private cause of action.

The scope of a statutory provision is determined by its language, and clear general language should not be narrowly confined merely because of the provision’s placement within a particular section or subdivision of the statute.
When Congress adopts a term drawn from the Constitution, the term is ordinarily understood to carry its established constitutional meaning in the statute.

When Congress authorizes a traditional common-law writ or uses an undefined common-law term, courts presume it carries its traditional common-law scope and should not read the statute to enlarge or alter that traditional function absent statutory language (or other clear indicia) showing an intent to do so.

When Congress repeatedly retains a statutory provision across successive enactments, that continuity may be relevant evidence that Congress intended the provision (and its established policy/purpose) to persist absent contrary indication.

When Congress uses expansive relational language (e.g., “relating to” or “in connection with”), courts should give that language its ordinary broad scope, while still reading it in statutory context and structure, and should not narrow it absent a textual or contextual basis.
Statutory (or other legal) provisions that use identical or materially identical language should generally be interpreted consistently.

When a statute (or similar legal instrument) requires an act to be done within a specified period from or after a particular day or event, the day of the event is excluded from the computation and the last day of the period is included.
When a statute amends an earlier statute, the amended provisions are read as part of the earlier statute as of the amendment’s effective date.

Where Congress authorizes a governmental purpose and delegates to the President (or another executive actor) the discretion to determine an implementing detail (such as the place), the executive’s choice within that delegation is treated, for legal-effect purposes, as equivalent to Congress having specified that detail in the statute (i.e., the action is "by authority of law").

When a statute confers discretion to implement a standard (e.g., a “reasonable” fee), that discretion and any interpretive choices should be exercised in a manner consistent with the statute’s evident purpose; applications that would depart from or undermine the statute’s aim (such as unjustified awards serving only to enrich attorneys) should be disfavored.

When a statute creates a general liability but provides no remedy, it may be enforced through an appropriate common-law action; but when the statute couples the liability with a special remedial scheme, that specified remedy is exclusive and must be followed.

When a statute expressly prohibits particular conduct (including entering a specified kind of contract), courts must give that prohibition controlling effect and will not enforce agreements made in direct violation of it (treating them as void).
When a statute is ambiguous, courts should avoid interpretations that unduly restrict the flexibility of government action.

When a statute is phrased in individualized terms (e.g., protecting or regulating ‘any individual’), it should be interpreted to require individualized application rather than decisions based solely on class-wide generalizations.

When a statute is silent, avoid inferring that Congress implicitly surveyed and adopted the then-prevailing legal rule at each enactment or revision—especially where that inference would create serious practical or administrability problems for courts applying different statutes enacted at different times.
When a statute provides an exclusive list of exemptions or exceptions, items not included in that list are not exempted (the express inclusion of some implies the exclusion of others).

When a statute requires a person to have “reasonable cause to believe” a fact, courts apply an objective prudent-person standard: whether the facts brought to the person’s notice would lead a prudent person in that position (e.g., prudent businesspeople/creditors in similar circumstances) to the relevant conclusion, regardless of actual knowledge or subjective belief.

When a statute requires a written memorandum, the writing must itself (or through a reference it contains to another writing) set out the essential terms; if the essential terms cannot be ascertained from the writing(s) in that way, the statute is not satisfied.

When a statute requires a “hearing,” that requirement implies the ordinary incidents of a hearing, including an opportunity to present evidence and a duty to decide in accordance with the evidence presented.

When a statute requires an act to be done within a specified number of days after (or from) an event, the provision sets a latest permissible time for compliance; performing the act earlier may still satisfy the statute so long as it is done no later than the deadline.

When a statute requires that an act be done with an intent to cause a prohibited result, a court may infer (or attribute) that intent where the act’s obviously necessary consequences are to produce that prohibited result, and may therefore treat the conduct as falling within the statutory description.

When a statute’s enforcement/remedial provisions expressly specify particular limitations on relief, courts generally should not infer additional unstated limitations—especially from provisions remote from the remedial authorization—absent clear textual indication that Congress intended such further limits.

When a statute’s text is unclear as to whether a particular fact is an offense element or a sentencing factor, courts may consult legal tradition and past congressional practice (as one indicator of congressional intent).

When a statutory term affects jurisdiction, courts should—because jurisdictional tests are often applied at the outset of a case—favor interpretations/tests that are as simple and readily administrable as possible, rather than unduly abstract, complex, or open-ended ones (consistent with the statute’s text, purpose, and precedent).

When construing the scope of primary liability under a statutory prohibition (e.g., who “makes” a false statement), courts may look to settled common-law principles (such as principal liability for acting through an innocent intermediary) and should not adopt an interpretation that creates a substantial departure or loophole absent support in the statute’s text, history, or precedent indicating Congress intended that result.
Where the rationale for a statutory rule does not apply, the rule itself does not apply in that circumstance.

Where a jurisdiction has a reception/default-law provision declaring the common law applicable, the common law governs unless and until it is displaced by an express contrary provision (or other specified overriding source, such as controlling federal/territorial law, local precedent, or established local usage).
A court may disregard statutory words as surplusage when they appear inadvertently inserted or are repugnant to the rest of the statute.
A court should not read a statute to deny, eliminate, or substantially curtail a power that the law otherwise confers merely because the power could be abused in practice.

A failure to comply with a formality (such as reducing an act to writing) does not invalidate an entity’s act unless the governing statute makes that formality indispensable (e.g., as evidence or to give the act obligatory force); but if the statute does impose such a requirement, it must be complied with.

If a statutory proviso (or exemption clause), after attempting to harmonize the statute’s parts, is irreconcilably repugnant to the enacting clauses it qualifies, the proviso is inoperative/void and cannot be applied to defeat those enacting clauses.
A special statutory exemption or privilege does not transfer with property unless the statute provides for such a transfer.

A specialized interpretive rule or term-construction adopted in a particular statutory domain (e.g., criminal tax law) because of features unique to that domain (e.g., the tax laws’ complexity) should not be extended to other statutes when those justifying features are absent.

A statute should not be read as having resolved a particular issue (or as reflecting a specific intent about it) when the statutory text, on its face, manifests no intention to address that issue and the pertinent legislative discussion shows no advertence to it; in that event, the issue must be resolved by reference to the statute’s purpose as disclosed by its structure.

A statute that expressly imposes particular duties (especially safety measures) should not be read, absent clear indication of exclusivity or displacement, to relieve a party of other applicable duties—such as the common-law duty to take whatever additional reasonable precautions the circumstances require.
A statute’s remedial provisions may be used to infer Congress’s intent or policy objectives underlying the statute.

A statutory term in a series may have a character of its own and should not automatically be “submerged” by neighboring words; however, its meaning must still be determined in context, and associated words may indicate that the series conveys a common idea (sometimes using overlapping, illustrative terms to enlarge rather than confine coverage).

A statutory term may take on a more demanding meaning in criminal statutes; in particular, although “willfully” can mean merely intentional/knowing/voluntary (as opposed to accidental), when used in a criminal statute it generally denotes action undertaken with a bad purpose and without justifiable excuse (and is sometimes associated with acting without grounds for believing the conduct lawful or in careless disregard of whether one has the right to act).

A subsequent statutory amendment does not necessarily imply that the pre-amendment statute excluded the amended subject; an amendment may be enacted to remove doubt (and thus be superfluous) and may reflect an intent to enlarge rather than restrict the prior law.
Absent a clear statutory indication, courts are reluctant to interpret criminal statutes as imposing liability based on negligence rather than a higher culpable mental state.

Absent a clear statutory statement to the contrary, courts presume that a statute does not authorize the imposition of punitive (or punitive-like) damages against governmental entities (including States).

When a statute grants an official the power to appoint an officer or employee, the power to remove the appointee is, absent statutory provision to the contrary, an incident of the power to appoint; and the power to suspend is an incident of the power to remove.
Absent a violation of a specific constitutional provision, a court should not refuse to apply retroactive civil legislation to its intended scope merely because the retroactive result seems unfair.

Absent an express temporal limitation, an enactment is presumed to continue in force until repealed or abrogated by competent authority; adding terms like “forever” does not alter that default legal effect.

Absent clear congressional intent, tax statutes should not be interpreted to permit a taxpayer to obtain a double deduction (or otherwise duplicative tax benefit) for the same economic loss or outlay.

Although ignorance of the law is ordinarily no defense, when an offense includes a legally defined status/characteristic as an element, a statute’s mens rea requirement may be interpreted to require knowledge of that legal-status element—so lack of such knowledge can be a defense.

When a statutory filing or claim asserts entitlement beyond what the statute authorizes, it should not be treated as wholly invalid if it can be given effect to the extent the statute authorizes; an overclaim does not forfeit the valid portion.

When Congress reenacts or continues statutory language, a prior administrative interpretation may be treated as carried forward only if that interpretation is clear, settled, and provides a definite criterion; ambiguous or equivocal regulations do not limit the meaning of reenacted statutory text, which instead presumptively retains the meaning it had in the prior statutes.
Courts can intervene to correct a misconstruction of the law by an administrative agency when such misconstruction denies parties their rightful claims.

Courts must follow clear congressional command regardless of consequences; but where the statute’s text and related indicia show Congress expressed a contrary policy, courts should avoid constructions that frustrate or “checkmate” that expressed congressional will.

Courts presume that statutes do not operate retroactively absent clear legislative intent—especially where retroactive application would disturb settled pre-enactment rights or obligations—and likewise disfavor finding that a later statute repeals an earlier one by implication.
Courts should apply the statute as enacted, not revise or supplement it based on what Congress might or should have done in light of policy considerations or external evidence.

Courts should be cautious about attaching substantial interpretive weight, standing alone, to minor grammatical or linguistic variations in statutory text (such as the use of “any” versus “the”), because Congress’s drafting is often inexact and such variations may not reflect a deliberate distinction.

Courts should begin with the statutory text; but even where language appears plain, they may look beyond a literal reading when the statute uses specialized terms with established federal meanings or operates within a complex statutory scheme, including considering long-standing agency interpretations and related statutory context.

To determine the boundaries of the field occupied by a federal statute for purposes of preemption, courts look to the federal statute itself, read in light of its constitutional setting and its legislative history.

Courts should not construe a federal criminal statute to make the existence of a crime (or criminal liability) depend on variable extra-statutory facts such as local law or local customs, unless Congress has explicitly and clearly directed that result.

Courts should not construe a statute’s requirements as yielding to, or being limited by, contrary private customs or contracts, where the statute is designed to set mandatory standards or confer statutory rights.

Courts should not lightly construe a statute to reach or burden activity protected by the First Amendment right to petition (and related associational rights) absent a clear indication that Congress intended that result.

Courts should not presume the legislature intended to confer an unfair procedural advantage on one party over another; where the statutory text fairly permits, courts should adopt the fair and reasonable interpretation that avoids such one-sided advantage.

Courts should presume the legislature intended to legislate only within its lawful authority, and should construe statutory language to reach the full extent of that authority unless the statute’s express language clearly indicates a narrower scope.

Do not read a statutory requirement to “state reasons” (or similar procedural commands) as demanding a full, detailed opinion in every case; the sufficiency of the explanation is context-dependent and must be enough to show reasoned decisionmaking and consideration of the parties’ nonfrivolous arguments.

Ecological (and similar policy) considerations may be invoked to resolve a genuine statutory indeterminacy—such as an inherent boundary-drawing ambiguity in applying a statutory term—but they are not an independent basis to extend statutory coverage to features that present no such ambiguity under the text.

Established interpretive canons—such as the rule against construing one statutory provision to render another superfluous, even across provisions enacted at different times—cannot be overridden by judicial speculation about legislators’ subjective intent in enacting a later provision.

Express statutory exclusions or limitations (especially in jurisdictional grants/waivers of sovereign immunity) must be enforced; courts should not extend a statute’s reach to excluded categories or permit evasion of the exclusion by recharacterizing an essentially excluded claim (e.g., a tort) as something else (e.g., implied contract).

Federal revenue statutes (and other federal statutes establishing a national scheme) are not presumed to incorporate or be governed by state law unless the statutory text or necessary implication so requires; when incorporation is necessarily implied, state law ordinarily determines the existence and content of the underlying property interests/rights, while federal law determines their tax consequences or federal characterization.
General statutory terms may be interpreted and applied with reference to their common sense meaning as informed by ordinary human experience.
Courts should not presume that officials will exercise delegated statutory discretion arbitrarily or unconstitutionally.

If a statute’s text and structure indicate it was expected to have general application, it should not be construed as though it were merely a special act—such as an amendment of the charters of particular private corporations.

If statutory text has a clear (plain) meaning, courts will not adopt (or defer to an agency’s) interpretation that contradicts that plain meaning; deference is appropriate only where the statute is silent or ambiguous and the agency’s interpretation is reasonable.

In construing a statute enacted to implement or conform domestic law to a treaty or protocol, courts may consult that international instrument—and the statute’s symmetry with it—as contextual evidence confirming the statute’s meaning, alongside the statutory text and other ordinary interpretive tools.

In deciding whether a statute implies a private civil cause of action, courts should not give undue weight to the presence of criminal penalties (particularly where the criminal provision is separate or broadly applicable), because criminal enforcement is not, by itself, strong evidence of an implied private remedy.
Committee reports and conference materials may carry greater interpretive weight than individual floor remarks or hearing testimony.
Interpretive materials should be read in context rather than in isolation; meaning should not be derived from decontextualized excerpts.

Interpretive rigor may differ between public (sovereign) grants and private grants; public grants are typically construed more strictly (in favor of the sovereign and against the grantee) than private grants.
Limitations provisions are generally interpreted and applied in light of their repose function—protecting parties from defending against stale claims after a legislatively specified period.

Official U. S. Code codification (in non–positive-law titles) is prima facie evidence of federal statutory law under 1 U. S. C. § 204(a); the Code’s placement/numbering may therefore support a rebuttable presumption about statutory meaning unless sufficiently persuasive contrary indications overcome it.

Provisions describing the effect of a conveyance (or of a public act transferring property) operate primarily as between the parties to that act and do not, by the grantor’s recitals or admissions, prejudice the rights or claims of third persons holding adverse title.
Repeal of a repealing statute can (and may be presumed to) revive the statute previously repealed, absent indication that Congress did not intend revival.
A statute should not be construed to require impossible compliance absent clear legislative direction.

Statutes should be interpreted in light of settled legal distinctions and traditional incidents of the relevant legal concepts; where Congress includes a provision characteristic of one established category (e.g., tolling, which traditionally applies to statutes of limitations), that inclusion can indicate the statute is limited to that category rather than a distinct category lacking that characteristic (e.g., statutes of repose).

Statutes should not be construed as transferring Congress’s legislative power to an agency’s unbounded discretion; courts should read and apply such statutes as imposing meaningful legal constraints and preserving judicial responsibility to ensure the agency follows statutory mandates.
Statutory interpretation should avoid results that are discriminatory or have far-reaching impacts that Congress likely did not intend.
Statutory provisions should be interpreted in light of the practical conditions and foreseeable contingencies that Congress would have contemplated when enacting the statute.
Statutory references to a 'person' may be construed to include artificial entities (such as corporations or bodies politic), not only natural individuals, depending on the statute’s usage.

Statutory requirements stated in mandatory terms cannot be reduced or negated by private contractual stipulations; courts should not construe statutes to permit contractual override of the statute’s positive terms.

Statutory silence in a federal scheme does not by itself require borrowing state law or limiting the operation of federal law; because legislation is inevitably incomplete, federal courts may fashion interstitial federal rules when necessary to fill gaps and effectuate the statutory patterns Congress enacted.

Statutory terms are ordinarily given their normal meaning (e.g., “or” is typically disjunctive), but that literal meaning may yield when the statute’s context and whole-text reading show that “or” is used carelessly as a substitute for “and” or otherwise indicate a different sense.
Statutory terms should be interpreted in light of their context, and a word’s meaning may vary depending on the statutory setting.

Substantial judicial disagreement (e.g., conflicts among circuits and differing decisions in other courts) can be evidence that a statutory provision is not clear or unambiguous in the direction one party claims.

The content of a criminal statute’s mens rea requirement (including whether the statute defines a “public welfare offense” and what category of regulated/dangerous items triggers a truncated mens rea) is a question of law for courts to determine through statutory interpretation; it may not be left to juries to define case by case, though juries may decide the factual question whether the defendant had the required knowledge as so defined.
When permissive language covers a special case, it is generally understood to prohibit what it does not authorize.
A word’s etymology may illuminate its meaning and the development of its usage.

To determine the scope of a statutory offense (and thus venue), courts should look to the acts Congress denounced in the statutory text and infer from the statute’s language where the prohibited conduct occurs.

Unless the statute indicates otherwise, statutory language is not read as speaking only as of the date of enactment; consistent with modern drafting convention, it “speaks” as of the time it is read—typically the time the operative conduct (or first act necessary for liability) occurs—reflecting the statute’s continuing application.
When Congress directs conformity with state law, state law supplies the rule for the covered subject, subject to controlling federal law.

When interpreting a provision that corresponds to or is drawn from another jurisdiction’s enactment, interpretations and commentary from the source jurisdiction regarding the corresponding provision may be consulted as persuasive evidence of meaning.

When Congress is considering legislation to authorize (or amend the law to permit) a particular power or rule, that fact may *suggest*—though not conclusively establish—that the power or rule is not authorized under existing law.

When Congress later carries forward or continues in statute the substance of an existing administrative regulation or settled interpretation, that later enactment may be treated as persuasive evidence—sometimes described as “declaratory”—of what Congress meant in the earlier statute.

When a cause of action or remedial feature is judicially implied from a statutory provision, courts may look to the most closely analogous express cause of action within the same statutory scheme and may borrow (or decline to borrow) elements from that analogue in determining what the implied action requires (e.g., whether reliance must be proven).

When a clear-statement rule functions as an implied limitation on otherwise unambiguous general statutory terms in a sensitive domain, courts should apply the limitation application-by-application—disallowing only those particular applications that intrude on the protected domain absent a clear statement—rather than treating the statute as wholly inapplicable (or nullifying an arbitrarily broader set of applications) because some applications would trench on that domain.

When a court or official acts under a special statutory power (especially one exercised in a special/summary manner outside ordinary common-law forms), the statute’s conditions must be satisfied and shown on the record, and courts will not presume compliance or jurisdiction beyond what distinctly appears.

When a criminal offense is complete upon the defendant’s act, it should not be construed as a continuing offense for venue purposes in every district affected by later transportation or downstream effects (e.g., each district through which goods pass), absent statutory and constitutional justification.
When a federal criminal statute requires “willfulness,” the Supreme Court generally interprets that requirement to demand proof that the defendant knew the conduct was unlawful.

When a federal statute implicates uniquely federal interests, especially foreign relations, and Congress has expressed an interest in uniform national rules, courts should not allow divergent state-law doctrines to supply the governing rule on matters the statute leaves unresolved; instead, they should apply a uniform federal rule (often federal common law).
Federal statutory offense classifications ordinarily depend on the federal statute, not varying state-law labels for the same conduct, absent contrary congressional intent.

When a general rule would treat acts done in violation of a statutory prohibition as void, that rule yields if, upon surveying the statute as a whole—its subject matter and the mischief it seeks to prevent—it appears the legislature intended a different consequence; courts must give effect to that intention.
Valid regulations issued under delegated statutory authority may clarify statutory duties and operate as part of the statutory scheme.

When a statute adopts ‘the common law’ by general reference, it is construed to incorporate the common law (and associated generally applicable statutes historically treated as part of that body), as of a defined historical time, limited to rules not inconsistent with superior or local law and suitable to local conditions.

When a statute requires an act to be performed by a known and responsible public officer, courts may infer that the officer must perform it personally (i.e., not by delegation) unless the statute indicates otherwise.

When a statute conditions jurisdiction on a monetary ‘amount’ or on the value of the ‘matter in dispute,’ the dispute must involve money or a right whose value can be calculated and ascertained in money; purely non-pecuniary controversies do not satisfy that requirement.

When a statute contains an express exception or exemption, courts may draw a negative implication that conduct outside the stated exception remains covered by the statute’s general prohibition or restriction (expressio unius / negative implication).

When a statute contains separable provisions, and the challenged enforcement in the case does not invoke a separable provision (such as a penalty clause), the court may adjudicate the validity and application of the invoked provisions while declining to express any opinion on the separable, uninvoked provision’s constitutionality.

When a statute creates a right and prescribes a remedy to enforce it, federal courts may follow the prescribed remedy (including in the same form as in state court) so long as the remedy is substantially consistent with the federal courts’ ordinary modes of proceeding (e.g., in chancery).

When a statute directs that a monetary threshold be computed “exclusive of interest,” courts should exclude interest demanded as a separate, accessory item, but should treat interest calculations that are merely components of the claimed damages as part of the principal demand for purposes of the statutory computation.

When a statute does not expressly prescribe an operational detail for administering a statutory system, a uniform, longstanding, and settled practice consistent with the statute’s scheme may be treated as having become part of the system—effectively supplying that detail for determining what counts as proper compliance (e.g., for notice purposes).
When a statute does not specify the standard for judicial review of agency action, courts apply the default standard supplied by the Administrative Procedure Act.
When a statute does not specify which court should have jurisdiction, the matter is determined by the ordinary rules of jurisdiction.

When a statute employs commerce-jurisdiction language such as “affecting commerce,” especially coupled with an expansive definition, it should be interpreted to extend to the full breadth of Congress’s power under the Commerce Clause unless the statute indicates a narrower scope.

When a statute enumerates an actor’s powers, one might infer that unenumerated or broader powers are excluded; but that negative inference does not apply where the statute expressly provides that enumerating powers does not exclude other powers.

When a statute enumerates multiple exceptions or criteria, courts should not treat one enumerated provision as the exclusive rule; they must consider the other enumerated provisions that may apply to the case and arguments presented.

When a statute uses a generic legal concept drawn from criminal law (e.g., “theft”), courts may consult the common-law background but should interpret the term in its generic, contemporary sense as reflected in the modern, widely adopted framework across American jurisdictions.

When a statute frames an outcome to turn on whether a specified decisionmaker (e.g., “the court”) “finds” or “determines” a matter, that wording may (though it does not compel) support an inference that Congress intended appellate courts to give some deference to that decisionmaker’s determination (e.g., review for abuse of discretion rather than de novo), depending on context and other indicia.

When a statute enumerates offenses by name, the offense terms are ordinarily read to refer to the crimes’ usual (generic) meaning, rather than to every jurisdiction-specific variant of those offenses.

When a statute is understood to incorporate general common-law (e.g., tort) principles and the statutory text and history do not clearly resolve the issue, courts should not presume Congress meant to freeze the background law as of enactment; if intervening legal developments have rendered an earlier rule obsolete, courts should be reluctant to read the statute to perpetuate that obsolete doctrine.

When a statute of limitations is framed in terms of legal remedies, equity will treat itself as bound by the statute in cases of concurrent jurisdiction; otherwise, equity may apply the limitation period only by analogy rather than as a direct statutory command.
When a statute prescribes specific interpretive guides or sources to be consulted in resolving a statutory question, courts should follow and give effect to those statutory interpretive instructions.

When a statute provides for judicial review of an agency decision, review is ordinarily confined to the agency’s existing administrative record rather than a new record created in the reviewing court.

When a statute provides that a remedy, penalty, or prohibition applies “in addition to” other provisions or “any other law,” that language is a strong indication that Congress intended the statute to operate cumulatively—to supplement rather than displace other applicable laws—absent contrary indication.

When a statute refers to a quantity “as” determined/estimated “according to law,” the reference is to the actual figure produced by the legally prescribed estimation procedure (the real amount as lawfully ascertained), not to an administratively convenient or fictitious measure for particular days or periods.

When a statute regulates only a specified subset of a common-law subject (e.g., contempts committed in the court’s presence), other instances not covered by the statute remain governed and punishable under the common law.
When a statute restricts its operation to conduct occurring “in this State,” that phrase ordinarily encompasses all territory within the State’s geographical boundaries (absent contextual narrowing).

When a statute turns on whether a fact is “material,” materiality is assessed objectively—by the significance of the fact to a hypothetical reasonable decisionmaker, not by the subjective reaction of an actual decisionmaker.

When a statute uses a general phrase like “required by law,” it is not necessarily limited to requirements stated in statutory text; the phrase may include binding requirements imposed by valid regulations (including state administrative regulations) promulgated pursuant to statutory authority, so long as the regulations are reasonably adapted to enforcing the statute and do not conflict with express statutory provisions.

When a statute uses a hierarchical structure (section/subsection/paragraph), a cross-reference at a given level ordinarily incorporates the material at that level; if Congress intends to cross-reference only a specific subsection or paragraph, it typically says so expressly.

When a statutory scheme’s structure and evident purpose make certain practical consequences foreseeable (e.g., evidentiary loss from delay), courts may infer Congress was aware of and accepted those consequences as part of the scheme, rather than treating them as an unintended defect warranting a judge-made override.

When an interpretation would effectively permit an unusual or structurally disruptive outcome (e.g., circumventing statutory quorum/delegation requirements), courts may be reluctant to infer that Congress authorized it through an indirect, unlikely, or convoluted textual mechanism; if Congress intended that outcome, it would likely have spoken in more straightforward terms.
When an offense is defined as a failure or neglect to perform a legal duty, the violation is treated as occurring where the duty should have been performed (and venue lies there).

When applying a statute’s remedial scheme (e.g., selecting remedies under the NLRA), the decisionmaker should choose remedies that reasonably effectuate the statute’s purposes and policies (consistent with any competing statutory constraints).
When applying an open-textured statutory standard, courts may construe and apply it in light of the statute's basic premise and Congress's articulated objectives.
When interpreting an unclear definitional phrase, the entire term being defined should be considered, not just part of it.

When deciding whether a state-law claim with an embedded federal issue supports federal-question (§ 1331) jurisdiction, courts should deny a federal forum if exercising jurisdiction would upset the congressionally approved (or assumed) division of labor between state and federal courts, absent a clear indication that Congress intended that shift.

When deciding whether a state-law claim with an embedded federal issue supports federal-question jurisdiction, courts should treat Congress’s failure to provide a private federal cause of action (or remedy) for violation of the federal statute as strong but not dispositive evidence that allowing federal jurisdiction (and thereby federal-court remedies) for that statutory violation would flout or undermine Congress’s intended enforcement scheme and the congressionally approved federal–state balance.

When determining what facts the prosecution must prove beyond a reasonable doubt, courts usually treat the legislature’s definition of the offense’s elements as dispositive, subject to constitutional limits.

When determining whether something falls within a statute’s protected/regulated category, courts may look to the statute’s underlying purpose—i.e., the kinds of interests or discoveries the statute was enacted to protect—and construe the statute’s scope accordingly.
When statutory language is construed as making a present grant (a grant in praesenti), the grant is interpreted to transfer title immediately upon enactment, not at some later time.

When statutory language is reasonably susceptible of more than one construction, courts should (where the text permits) adopt the interpretation that best respects and accommodates relevant constitutional safeguards or policies (here, the Sixth Amendment’s venue/vicinity protection).
When statutory language is unclear and authoritative guidance is lacking, courts should prefer an interpretation that accords with familiar and well-settled principles of law.

When statutory text declares that a specified instrument or determination is “conclusive evidence” of a described right or fact, courts generally treat it as conclusively establishing that right or fact within the scope of the statutory declaration (i.e., as an irrebuttable showing), and give the language its stated legal effect.

When the governing statute does not clearly require a particular result and instead leaves room for policy judgment within statutory limits, courts should leave the initial resolution of such interpretive/policy questions to the administering agency’s informed judgment—and should not preempt that judgment by dictating either the substantive outcome or an unreasonably narrow procedural context for the agency’s initial decision.

When the substantive offense, by its nature, necessarily requires the concerted participation of two persons for its commission, and the only agreement alleged is the agreement inherent in committing that offense, the Government may not evade the statute’s built-in limitations by charging the parties with a separate conspiracy absent evidence that the legislature intended cumulative conspiracy liability.

Where Congress creates a federal equitable right and the statute is silent as to a limitations period, courts generally apply traditional (historic) equitable timeliness principles (such as laches), rather than borrowing and applying a different jurisdiction’s statute of limitations as the controlling measure.
Where a statute defines an offense in terms of a fraudulent “scheme,” it does not require proof that the fraud was completed or succeeded; the scheme itself is the punishable conduct.

A claim of statutory ambiguity is strongest when competing meanings are accepted and reflected across many standard sources (e.g., multiple dictionaries), whereas a meaning found only in a lone, out-of-step dictionary—especially one that contradicts the prevailing definitions—is a weak basis for finding ambiguity.

A claimant can take a statutory benefit only by fitting within the class the statute itself describes; an external document (such as a will) cannot expand or redefine the statutory category unless the statute makes that description controlling.

A court may treat statutory language as a legal term of art only if the asserted term of art (as such) actually appears in the statute being construed; courts may not import, rearrange, or substitute different wording to manufacture a term-of-art reading.
A later authoritative judicial construction is read into the statute from its inception when determining earlier statutory rights.

A court’s jurisdiction is presumed to be confined to the territorial limits assigned to it by its creating law and does not extend beyond those boundaries (e.g., beyond the department), unless the law clearly provides otherwise.
A direct conflict between statutory commands should not be treated as mere ambiguity to be resolved by interpretation; choosing between conflicting commands is a legislative, not interpretive, act.
A general statute intended to be of general application applies to newly created rights of the same class (e.g., new rights of appeal) unless the legislature provides otherwise.
Omission of express judicial review may suggest its absence, but the inference is weakened when background law supplies review.
A power to revoke or impair contractual or vested rights will not be implied from general statutory authority; such a power must be reserved or delegated in clear, unmistakable, express terms.

A statute (or comparable legal instrument) should not be invalidated or denied effect merely because it fails to recite—or misrecites—the particular legal authority for its issuance; the proper inquiry is whether some valid authority exists to support it.
Provisions imposing burdens are construed strictly, while provisions conferring relief are construed liberally.
A statute may require affirmative proof of a fact even when that fact would otherwise be presumed.

A statute of limitations may be given effect even if part of the relevant period has already elapsed, so long as a reasonable time remains to sue or act; in such circumstances, the remaining reasonable time is treated as the legislature’s contemplated limitation.

A statute should not be interpreted to permit an agency to deny regulatory approvals or impose categorical exclusions by arbitrarily discriminating among similarly situated regulated parties unless the statute contemplates or authorizes that discriminatory treatment.

A statute that authorizes an injured party (and only that party or their representative) to recover damages for violation of the party’s rights is ordinarily construed as remedial rather than penal, even if it sets minimum or enhanced damages.
A statute will not be read to abrogate tribal sovereign immunity unless Congress clearly and unequivocally expresses its intent to do so.

A statute will not be read to displace the Federal Arbitration Act’s requirement that arbitration agreements be enforced (even for federal statutory claims) unless another statute contains a contrary congressional command overriding the FAA’s mandate.
An express grant of exclusive federal jurisdiction may indicate that Congress intended federal courts to supply the forum and develop the statute’s jurisprudence.
A statutory definition that states what a term “means” is usually exhaustive and excludes meanings not included in the definition.

A statutory power is not forfeited or extinguished merely because it has gone long unexercised; long nonuse may warrant close scrutiny of whether the power was actually granted, but if granted it is not lost by dormancy—nor can an ungranted power be acquired by an unchallenged exercise.

A statutory prohibition should not be construed as inapplicable merely because the prohibited conduct is undertaken pursuant to, or justified by, a private contractual provision; parties may not use contract terms as a defense to engage in conduct that would otherwise violate the statute where doing so would undermine the statutory protection Congress established.
A statutory provision that creates a rebuttable presumption does not, without clear language, enlarge the scope of the underlying substantive statutory predicates.

A statutory provision that merely authorizes reimbursement (or compensation) for undertaking an action does not, by itself, imply that the reimbursable action is mandatory; any duty to undertake it must be found in other, duty-imposing statutory text.

Absent a specific statutory provision to the contrary, federal income tax items are personal to the taxpayer: income is reported (and taxed) to the person who earns it, and deductions are taken only by the taxpayer who incurs the expense or sustains the loss—not by third parties.
Administrative practice that predates a statute is not relevant to determining the meaning of that statute.

An interpreter should not infer that a statute or regulation bars a permissible course of action or narrowing construction (especially by the authorized decisionmaker) unless the text itself imposes that prohibition or limitation.

An issue-exhaustion or objection-preservation bar is construed to apply only to objections that were available and could have been raised in the prior proceeding; it does not preclude judicial consideration of an objection based on circumstances that arose only after the agency proceeding, because the party could not have raised a then non-existent issue.

At common law, repeal of a statute abates the government’s power to prosecute for violations committed while the statute was in force; but that rationale does not apply where only an implementing regulation is revoked while the underlying statute—and its continuing policy creating the offense and penalties—remains in force.

Because the ultimate meaning of generally applicable legal texts that bind the public at large (e.g., statutes—and, by analogy, patent claims) should not turn on the case-specific evidentiary record, that ultimate meaning should be treated as a legal determination not dependent on the particular evidence presented in a given case (often reinforced by de novo appellate review).
Congress likely would express a significant policy decision in plain statutory language or at least in affirmative legislative history statements.

Congress’s codification or compilation of statutes, without reenactment of the relevant provision, does not by itself imply legislative adoption of a particular judicial decision interpreting that provision.
Legal texts are interpreted by their objective public meaning rather than their authors’ private intentions.
Courts are bound by the meaning of the words Congress enacted, read in light of pertinent legislative history.

Courts ordinarily accept a state court’s construction of a state statute, but they need not do so where the construction is so strained or “fanciful” as to be unreasonable and effectively a subterfuge; statutory terms should not be given implausible meanings.

Courts should not automatically infer a substantive change in meaning from the inclusion of qualifying language, because legal drafters sometimes add qualifiers redundantly for emphasis even when the text would mean the same without them.

Courts should not construe an omissions provision as a general, freestanding duty of disclosure; it creates liability only when the omission of a material fact makes an affirmative statement actually made misleading (to a reasonable reader in context).
Courts should not impose an unsupported heightened clear-statement requirement before recognizing that an amendment changed prior judicially settled law.
Courts should not infer a broad statutory rule or blanket presumption from a narrow, circumscribed statement in legislative history, especially where the statutory text points the other way.

Courts should not treat statutes as implicitly delegating open-ended lawmaking discretion to the judiciary; instead, courts must adopt the statute’s single most plausible interpretation rather than choose among merely reasonable alternatives.
Criminal prohibitions are generally construed not to apply to reasonable law-enforcement actions undertaken by officers in the course of their duties.
Criminal statutes are generally construed (as a matter of assumed legislative intent) not to cover violations produced by government entrapment.

Do not construe a statute or treaty provision to require production of an original written instrument (or its record) as an absolute condition of proof or relief when the instrument has been lost or accidentally destroyed without the claimant’s voluntary or intentional act, absent clear textual indication that secondary (parol) evidence is barred.
Enumerated statutory exceptions may assist interpretation, but they do not, standing alone, define the scope of the general rule from which they are excepted.
Different elements of a statutory offense may require different mental states; a ruling about one element does not govern the others.
Foreign judicial decisions are a perilous basis from which to draw sure (firm) inferences about U.S. congressional intent in enacting a statute.
General statements of statutory purpose (or generalized rationales) are of limited value in determining the meaning or scope of a specific statutory provision, particularly a specific exception.

If Congress, by appropriate means of expression (e.g., by incorporating a definition in the enacted text or providing a contemporaneously authoritative explanation such as a conference report), clearly indicates that statutory language is to bear an unlikely or even odd meaning, courts should give effect to that congressional meaning rather than default to ordinary English usage.
If a later enactment is merely an amendment to an earlier statute, repeal of the original statute can operate to repeal the amendment as well.
If a statute regulates an area in which the federal interest is dominant, courts may infer that Congress intended federal law to preclude state laws on the same subject.

If an amendment expands a statute beyond what the prior text plainly covered, a court should treat the amendment as a substantive change and should not justify applying the expanded duty retroactively (including to impose criminal liability) by labeling the amendment “clarifying” or “declaratory.”

If statutory text and structure are ambiguous, an inference from the statute’s silence or omission carries interpretive weight only if the statute’s underlying legislative policy or purpose clearly supports that construction.

In applying statutory terms like “without compensation,” the absence of a separately stated fee for the specific act is not dispositive; interpreters should ask whether the act is performed as part of a paid arrangement or otherwise yields a concrete economic benefit (e.g., increased profitability) to the actor, rather than presuming compensation from the mere existence of a business relationship.
In construing penal statutes, later enactments repeal former ones that cover the same acts but impose a lesser penalty.
In construing statutes with criminal consequences, courts apply strict construction—resolving statutory doubt in favor of the accused.

In determining the scope or application of a statutory or jurisdictional scheme, a court may consider the legislation leading to its establishment and judicially noticeable surrounding circumstances to infer the scheme’s evident purpose.

In fee-shifting statutes, “prevailing party” status turns on whether the plaintiff obtained a material alteration of the parties’ legal relationship of the kind Congress sought to promote through the fee statute.
Courts should not exercise jurisdiction where reasonable doubts remain about its statutory legality.
Statutory requirements connected by and are ordinarily cumulative.

In interpreting a statute, courts may consider whom the statute is addressed to, and assess the statute’s requirements and practical application from the perspective of its intended addressee rather than outsiders.

In some public-welfare/regulatory criminal statutes, some courts have construed mens rea terms like “knowingly” to require awareness of the relevant conduct/facts but not awareness that the conduct is unlawful; however, this public-welfare rationale is narrow and may be inappropriate where penalties are serious, and it should not be invoked too readily.

In statutory text, a requirement that something be “prescribed by law” is ordinarily read to mean prescribed by legislative enactment (positive law), not by judicially devised standards of what is reasonable or just.

Inferring that a statute impliedly creates a cause of action does not, without further statutory indication, imply additional procedural or remedial directives (such as displacing the ordinary method for selecting a limitations period); courts should follow the standard default rules unless the statute supports a different consequence.
Legislative history should not be read to impute to Congress an implausibly broad or extreme statutory purpose beyond what the materials reasonably support.
Municipal security statutory requirements should not be technically construed and limited as to create traps for those who wish to invest in municipal securities.

Once legislative intent (ascertained from the statute’s text, context, and purpose) establishes the statute’s meaning, a court may not adopt an alternative meaning outside that intent merely because it would be more favorable to the taxpayer (i.e., would reduce the tax burden).
Precatory or hortatory statutory language is ordinarily interpreted as expressing a preference or aspiration, not as creating a binding legal mandate.

Private or individualized acts of Congress are not ordinarily treated as establishing, amending, or substituting for generally applicable statutory rules; courts should not infer a general legal rule from private relief legislation absent an enacted general statute.

Procedural forms or specimen/illustrative charging examples (and similar nonbinding guidance) should not be treated as creating substantive offenses, nor as providing a definitive or authoritative construction of the scope of a statute’s prohibitions.
Provisions addressing the same subject matter should be read together (in context with related sections) to determine meaning.

Provisions enacted in annual appropriations acts (including appropriations riders) are generally construed as effective only for the covered fiscal year, not as permanent legislation, unless Congress clearly indicates a continuing, permanent effect.

Provisions in related enactments addressing the same problem may sometimes shed indirect light on the meaning of the statute being construed, but only when the comparison supplies a reliable aid to construction rather than merely debating points.

Provisions within the same statute—especially those using similar operative language—should generally be interpreted consistently with one another, while differences in wording among subsections are presumed intentional and may warrant different meanings.
Public statutes are presumed known to all persons; everyone is charged with constructive knowledge of a public law’s provisions.
Reported congressional debates are not reliable evidence of statutory meaning; the enacted text governs.
Without sufficiently imperative statutory language, a statute need not exclude consideration of relevant circumstances in every case.
Statutes are not construed to confer corporate existence by implication; presumptions in statutory construction run against finding an implied grant of corporate existence.
Statutes of repose are ordinarily construed as establishing an outer deadline for suit that is not subject to equitable tolling or analogous equitable timing doctrines.

Statutes waiving sovereign immunity are strictly construed, but courts must not construe the waiver unduly restrictively or narrow the waiver beyond what Congress intended (and may apply equitable tolling where consistent with congressional intent).

Statutory (and regulatory) language should be interpreted in context and in light of its evident purpose; where a provision lists specific classes and then contains language indicating broader coverage, it may be read to extend the rule’s benefit beyond the expressly named classes to other persons whose duties fall within the stated functional criterion.

Statutory jurisdictional or review-triggering conditions (e.g., that the “validity” of a statute be “drawn in question”) turn on the substantive reality of the issue actually presented and decided, not on formal labels or the mere recitation of particular words as a “magic formula.”
Statutory language is ordinarily read according to its normal (ordinary) meaning as a starting point; if the text is ambiguous, a reasonable agency interpretation may be entitled to deference.
Statutory language should be interpreted in light of the legal context and background rules in place at the time of the statute’s enactment.
Interpreters should not categorically exclude traditional interpretive tools (text, structure, history and purpose) through an a priori rule.

Statutory meaning should be determined using the ordinary tools of statutory construction; courts should not adopt atextual (uncodified) narrowing limitations that lack support in the statute’s text, context, and related interpretive materials.

Statutory provisions authorizing appellate review should not be read to permit reexamination of facts found by a jury beyond the common-law modes of review (and the Seventh Amendment baseline) unless Congress clearly provides otherwise; a jury verdict conclusively determines issues of fact and is reviewable only for legal error.

Statutory terms should not be given a meaning dictated by specialized industry usage; trade usage may be considered, but it is not conclusive and cannot override common parlance and indicia of congressional intent (including legislative history and statutory structure).

Statutory text is ordinarily read according to its most natural (ordinary) meaning; however, if the most natural reading would render the statute unconstitutional, courts have a duty—if fairly possible—to adopt an alternative reasonable construction that saves the statute.
Statutory text should be interpreted against the backdrop of established legal tradition and practice in the relevant field.
Tax laws are generally understood to require payment in money unless the statute expresses a different intent (e.g., authorizing collection of taxes in kind or otherwise than money).
Tax statutes should be interpreted to give a uniform application to a nationwide scheme of taxation.
The phrase 'at any time' in a statute suggests flexibility and does not imply a requirement for continuity or past practice.

The presumption against pre-emption is pertinent in cases asking whether federal law pre-empts state law, but it has no force in federal–federal preclusion cases (where one federal statute is alleged to displace a cause of action under another) because the state–federal balance does not frame the inquiry.
The presumption that statutes do not bind the sovereign applies only with respect to the sovereign that enacted the statute (the enacting sovereign).

The term “laws” in the Constitution and federal statutes should not be read as limited solely to legislative enactments unless the text expressly so provides or the surrounding context indicates that limitation.

Traditional courts of equity do not enforce penalties or award punitive damages unless a statute expressly authorizes such relief; therefore, “equitable relief” ordinarily excludes punitive/penal remedies absent express statutory authorization.
Venue provisions in federal criminal statutes should not be construed so expansively, absent clear congressional direction, as to give the Government undue discretion to choose a favorable forum.

When Congress adopts statutory language reflecting a judicially used standard (e.g., a particular circuit’s formulation), it does not necessarily codify that jurisdiction’s prior case law interpreting the standard.

When Congress amends statutory language to conform more closely to an existing, settled judicial interpretation of similar language, the amendment may be read as aligning with—and in some cases codifying or making explicit—that interpretation.

When Congress enacts a federal statute of general application intended to occupy the field (or achieve constitutionally required uniformity) on a subject, that statute is construed to supersede state-law remedies and other gap filling rules.

When Congress enacts a statute against the backdrop of (or with reference to) an earlier agency decision, the relevant interpretive question is how Congress understood that earlier decision at the time of enactment, not what the agency subjectively meant when it issued the earlier decision.

When Congress enacts a statute in response to a decision holding a prior version unconstitutional, the statute should be construed—consistent with its text and evident object—as limited to the constitutionally authorized sphere Congress sought to reach (here, lawful foreign and Indian commerce), rather than extended to constitutionally doubtful local commerce.

When Congress establishes a distinct, detailed, and self-sufficient procedure for a particular class of cases, courts should not extend a more general or differently situated procedural power from another part of the statute into that area—especially where the two procedures are inconsistent or would create conflict.

When Congress includes an express pre-emption provision in a federal statute, that inclusion ordinarily indicates a particular congressional interest in preventing States from enacting laws that might interfere with Congress’ statutory objectives.

When Congress reenacts or carries forward materially similar statutory language after the Executive has openly and repeatedly exercised (or asserted) a particular authority under predecessor statutes with substantially the same language, that reenactment supports an inference that Congress has acquiesced to or ratified that executive authority.

When Congress uses different statutory formulations within the same statutory scheme—especially when some provisions contain qualifying language that cannot sensibly describe the elements of a generic offense—courts should infer that those provisions may require different interpretations or interpretive methods (e.g., categorical versus circumstance-specific).
An express statutory direction to reexamine agency findings can require broader review than merely checking general standards.

When a defendant commits a series of discrete, successive violations of a legal duty, the statute of limitations generally runs separately for each violation, so each act can give rise to its own timely claim if within the limitations period.

When a federal statute authorizes resort to federal court but does not specify the procedure for invoking the court’s jurisdiction (i.e., how the proceeding is commenced), the generally applicable Federal Rules of Civil Procedure govern, absent a contrary statutory directive.

When a federal statute creates a claim against the United States, a judicial remedy does not automatically follow; a court remedy exists only if, from the nature and character of the legislation, Congress intended the statutory claim or privilege to be protected by judicial remedies.
Claims primarily within an agency’s statutory competence should first be presented to that agency before judicial enforcement.
A general statutory right of appeal applies as the tribunal’s jurisdiction expands, absent a special procedure or clear limitation.

When a jurisdictional (or removal) statute requires that the “matter in dispute” or “sum in controversy” exceed a specified amount, the amount in controversy is determined from the damages demanded in the initiating pleadings; a later recovery below the threshold does not retroactively defeat federal jurisdiction (though it may affect costs).

When a jurisdictional amount-in-controversy requirement applies, costs and post-judgment interest are excluded from the jurisdictional-sum calculation because costs are not part of the matter in dispute and post-judgment interest arises only after rendition; when the amount in controversy is measured by the judgment, it is fixed at rendition.

When a later statute merely imposes a prohibition/limitation on a preexisting legal rule or authority, repeal of that prohibitory provision restores the law/authority as it existed before the prohibitory statute—unless the repealing statute itself, or a general governing statute, limits the repeal’s effect to simple abrogation (i.e., prevents such restoration).

When a legal issue arises within a regime created and governed by statute, the controlling answer should be derived from the relevant statutes and duly authorized rules promulgated pursuant to statute.
Authority for a municipality to incur debt ordinarily implies taxing authority sufficient to pay it, absent contrary legislative limits.

When a limitations statute applies to “bringing” a “civil action,” that phrase refers to filing a judicial lawsuit in a court of competent jurisdiction (not pursuing administrative proceedings), unless the statute indicates otherwise.
When a long line of Supreme Court precedent interpreting a similar statutory requirement has been left undisturbed by Congress, courts presume Congress intended to follow that established course.

When a penal statute does not expressly impose a penalty or extend liability to a particular class of persons (especially a necessary participant/victim contemplated by the statutory scheme), courts may draw a strong implication that the legislature did not intend to impose that penalty or liability on that class.

When a person has done everything the law requires to perfect or obtain a statutory right, the law should not treat that right as lost or defeated solely because a public officer’s misconduct or neglect prevented completion of the final official steps.
When a state statute of limitations is applied to a federal right, it should operate uniformly with respect to state and federal rights and provide a reasonable time to bring suit.

When a statute and its legislative history are silent on how to allocate burdens of proof, a court may consider policy considerations (including convenience and fairness) and adopt the allocation that best effectuates the statute’s purpose.
The permissive term 'may' indicates discretionary authority rather than a mandatory duty.

When a statute authorizes review of “questions of law,” that term can encompass the application of a legal standard to established (or undisputed) facts, not merely abstract or ‘pure’ legal questions.

When a statute conditions legal consequences on a person’s intent (e.g., acting "in contemplation" of some event), the required intent must accompany the person’s relevant act that gives legal effect to the transaction, rather than arising only afterward while others act.

When a statute covers myriad violations and prescribes only a maximum penalty, the maximum alone does not indicate what penalties within that range Congress thought appropriate for particular violations, and thus is a weak basis for inferring Congress’s relative assessment of the seriousness of specific conduct.

When a statute defines a single crime and divides it into degrees, the division is ordinarily understood as classifying the same offense for purposes of grading punishment based on aggravating circumstances, rather than creating separate offenses, absent clear statutory text to the contrary.

When a statute expressly makes the operation or validity of one provision contingent on the validity of other provisions (e.g., via a nonseverability/conditional-effect clause), courts should give effect to that instruction: if the specified provisions are held invalid, the linked provision is rendered invalid or remains operative only as the legislature directed (including restoring prior law if the statute so provides).
When a statute expressly provides that contractual waivers of statutory compliance are void, courts should not enforce private agreements that purport to waive compliance with the statute.
Bankruptcy rights, priorities, and estate property fixed as of a statutory date are determined as of that date.

When a statute is administered by an agency, and the statute leaves room for interpretation, a court may defer (in the first instance) to the agency’s reasonable determination that a particular burden-shifting or similar procedural framework is appropriate under that statute.

When a statute is phrased as an evidentiary presumption (especially a conclusive presumption), courts should look to its operative effect and the substantive policy it implements; such a “presumption” may function as a substantive rule of law rather than a mere rule of evidence.

If a constitutional right requires a particular procedural protection (e.g., a hearing), the statute should be construed—so far as fairly possible—in harmony with the Constitution to recognize and respect that right rather than to deny it; the Constitution and statute are construed together as one law.

When a statute makes eligibility or consequences turn on what a sentence was “based on,” courts should follow the text’s indicated focus by looking to the district court’s reasons/analytic framework for the sentence it imposed (including what served as its starting point), rather than to the parties’ reasons for their plea agreement or other extratextual considerations.
When a statute makes liability turn on acting “voluntarily,” the term may be construed to require knowledge of the relevant circumstances, rather than mere inadvertent or unaware conduct.

When a statute of limitations is imposed by law and the law also imposes a legal disability that makes suit impossible during a period, the statute should be construed, by necessary implication, to exclude (toll) the disability period from the limitations calculation so that neither the right to sue is extinguished while suit is barred nor the defendant is left without any limitations protection.

When a statute of limitations is triggered by an event, the trigger is ordinarily understood to be the alleged occurrence of that event for purposes of filing suit, rather than requiring proof that the event actually occurred.

When a statute or ordinance contains separable provisions, later legislative repeal or modification of separably operative, valid provisions does not impliedly ratify a distinct invalid provision—especially where the invalid provision is one the legislature could not have authorized or delegated in the first instance.
When statutory consequences turn on punishment, classification ordinarily depends on the punishment authorized, not the sentence imposed.

When a statute prescribes independent penalties (e.g., fine and imprisonment), the natural inference is that the legislature intended each penalty to apply so far as possible; if one penalty cannot be imposed on a particular defendant, that does not imply the statute is wholly inapplicable or that the defendant is exempt from the remaining penalty.
When a statute prescribes procedures to inform decisionmaking, it should not be interpreted to mandate particular substantive outcomes absent clear statutory language to that effect.
