When a statute prescribes the time within which an appeal (or similar review) must be taken, a court cannot permit the appeal to be filed after the statutory period has expired.
A statutory command that a convicted person shall receive a specified sanction makes that sanction mandatory.

When a statute provides that a specified tax or payment is imposed “in lieu of” other taxes or payments, that language indicates the specified charge is a substitute for, and displaces, the other charges within its stated scope.
When a statute provides that an action may be brought within a specified period after a disability is removed, the limitations period begins to run when the relevant disability is removed.

When a statute provides that imprisonment shall follow a trial and conviction, it is necessarily understood as intending that the imprisonment be inflicted as punishment for the offense of which the defendant was convicted.

When a statute requires a written instrument to be “signed,” the signature requirement is satisfied so long as the signatory’s name appears with the purpose/effect of authenticating the instrument as a whole, and it generally is not essential that the signature appear in any particular location in the document.

When a statute requires a “writing” (e.g., a “note or memorandum in writing”), that requirement may be satisfied by legible written inscription in forms such as printing or writing in lead pencil, absent a statutory indication to the contrary.

When a statute requires “consent” without specifying that it must be “express,” courts generally should not add an express-consent requirement absent textual or contextual indication that Congress imposed one.
When a statute uses a comparative threshold term like “exceeds,” it requires a strict greater-than showing and does not include an amount that is merely equal to the threshold.

When a statute uses a term (e.g., “position”) that the statutory text indicates includes particular incidents or components (such as seniority, status, and pay), a directive referring to that term (e.g., a bar on “discharge from such position”) should be read to apply to the position as so constituted—protecting those components and not merely the bare job slot.

When a statute uses broad terms to prohibit specified kinds of “conditions, agreements, or understandings,” a court may treat provisions that lack an express prohibited covenant as covered when, in context, their practical effect is functionally equivalent and of the same nature as the conduct the statute addresses.

When a statute uses “by means of” (e.g., § 1344(2)), the phrase requires more than but-for causation: the misrepresentation or false statement must function as the means—i.e., the mechanism or instrumentality in the ordinary course—by which the defendant obtains the relevant property, rather than being only a tangential or fortuitous cause of the result.

When a statute uses “including” after a general term, the items that follow are ordinarily understood as illustrative examples or members of that broader category (often non-exhaustive), not as additional, separate categories added to it as if “including” meant “and” or “as well as.”
When a statute or regulation contains no express limitation on the exercise of a power, it may be construed as implicitly limited by a requirement of reasonableness.
Courts should be reluctant to construe a statute as delegating the taxing power to an administrative agency.
General statutory terms may be narrowed to avoid unjust, oppressive, or unconstitutional results, with implied exceptions where supported.
When a statute’s meaning is doubtful, Congress’s construction of the statute—as evidenced by later legislative action—may be examined as an aid to interpretation.

When a statute’s operation depends on whether a revolutionary regime constitutes a “foreign prince or state” (i.e., a newly independent foreign state), courts do not decide that question for themselves; they follow the Government’s recognition determinations, and until recognition (by the United States or by the prior sovereign) courts must treat the prior sovereign status (“the ancient state of things”) as continuing.

When a statute’s text and structure describe recovery for “the injury” and provide that “the amount” recovered is to be “divided” among beneficiaries, that singular phrasing and apportionment mechanism indicate the statute contemplates a single cause of action and single liability for one injury with one lump-sum recovery, later allocated among entitled persons, rather than multiple separate recoveries.

When a statute’s text defines a predicate by reference to a generic offense category, courts generally apply a categorical (elements-based) approach; when the text instead uses circumstance-specific language, courts may look to case-specific circumstances to apply the statutory threshold.
When a statutory exception is incorporated into the enacting clause defining a criminal offense, the prosecution must plead and prove that the defendant does not fall within the exception.

When an earlier statutory section consists of a single, non-severable provision, a later statute that repeals it to the extent it falls within the later statute’s scope (or “purview”) cannot be applied partially; if the provision is repealed at all, the entire section is repealed.

When applying a statute that criminalizes speech, courts should construe the statutory term (e.g., “threat”) in light of First Amendment background principles and determine whether the defendant’s words qualify by considering the statement in its full context (including conditionality and audience reaction), not by isolating the words alone.

When comparing related statutory schemes, Congress’s express authorization (or non-authorization) of particular defenses—especially in conjunction with the presence or absence of a statute of limitations—can be relevant context in determining whether an equitable defense like laches is available under a different statute.

When construing (or designing under) a statutory religious accommodation, the interpreter should ensure the accommodation is measured and takes “adequate account” of burdens it would impose on nonbeneficiaries/third parties, so that it does not override other significant interests or the rights of those third parties.

When construing a federal statute enacted to exercise a constitutional power, absent an express contrary indication, courts should presume that what the statute directs to be done is to be carried out under federal (Union) authority and by federal institutions/tribunals, rather than by state organs.

When construing a statute that conditions a forfeiture or fixed sum on noncompliance, courts may look to whether the provision is framed in mandatory, law-imposing terms (an exercise of legislative power) rather than in bargained-for contractual terms.

When construing a statute that grants an agency procedural or administrative discretion, courts should read the statute (where the text permits) to allow reasonable procedures adapted to fair and orderly administration that are consistent with the statute’s policies and purposes.

When construing a statute, courts may give respectful consideration to widespread lower-court interpretations, but the persuasiveness of such interpretations depends on their reasoning, and numerical repetition alone does not establish correctness.

When construing a statute’s procedural/burden-of-proof provisions, and where the statutory text permits, courts may consider conventional rules of fairness and convenience—especially as to which party has readier access to particular evidence and what weight or scrutiny to give that evidence—provided those considerations are applied to the specific proof at issue.

When construing statutory language, a qualifying phrase should not be treated as restricting or describing the class covered if, in context, it is better read as declaring a duty or obligation applicable to those within the class.

When interpreting a statute that imposes a tax or liability, the method used to calculate the amount (the measure or base) does not itself determine the legal incidence or taxable event; the taxable event is identified by the statute’s operative description of what is being taxed or regulated.

When interpreting a statute’s scope—especially its potential to preempt or supersede state law—courts should consider other statutes that supply applicable presumptions or clear-statement rules (e.g., McCarran-Ferguson) as relevant evidence of congressional intent.
The historical origins and usage of a statutory term of art may illuminate the meaning the legislature adopted.
When interpreting statutes, courts should consider how other branches of government have addressed the same problem, especially in complex cases with many difficult questions.

When legally operative language measuring time using terms such as “from” a date/day is ambiguous as to whether the referenced day is included, courts may construe the day as inclusive or exclusive based on the subject matter and to give effect to the instrument and further justice; in statutes taking effect “from and after” their passage—especially where citizens’ rights are materially affected—courts may as a general rule exclude the day of passage unless inclusion is necessary to give the law effect.

When public (governmental) authority is conferred on several persons or a multi-member board to be exercised for public purposes, it is ordinarily exercisable by a majority of their number (unlike private joint agencies, which generally require joint action by all).

When specific examples precede an otherwise unqualified general term, ejusdem generis is only a fallback; if there is a special contextual reason for listing the specifics (e.g., ex abundanti cautela), that reason can negate any inference that the general term was meant to be limited to items ejusdem generis.
Practical consequences may guide statutory interpretation only when the statutory text is ambiguous.

When statutory text directs attention to the time a “cause of action” (or “claim”) arose—a time before a lawsuit is filed—courts may infer that the relevant “cause of action/claim” is conceptually distinct from, and should not be defined by, the relief demanded in the subsequently filed pleading.
When the existence of federal removal jurisdiction is doubtful, the doubt is resolved against removal and the case is remanded to state court.

When the found facts bring a case within a statutory or regulatory rule whose duty is plainly prescribed, courts should apply that rule as written; a party seeking departure based on a recognized exception or “special circumstances” bears the burden to establish facts bringing the case within that exception.

When the government does not invoke (or expressly waives) Chevron deference, a court generally should not apply Chevron sua sponte; instead, it should decide the statute’s meaning using its own best independent judgment.

When two provisions of the same statute are genuinely irreconcilable after reasonable efforts to harmonize them, the provision that appears later in the enactment may be treated as the legislature’s latest expression of intent and given controlling effect.
Where Congress has not specified the mental element of a crime, courts may infer a mens rea requirement based on common-law tradition.

Where a statute (especially a pre-emption clause) expressly covers both “requirements” and “prohibitions,” courts should treat state-law duties that are merely converses of one another (an affirmative mandate versus an equivalent negative ban) as equally within the statute’s scope, so the statute cannot be circumvented by recasting a requirement as a prohibition or vice versa.
Widespread judicial acceptance of an interpretation does not justify adopting that interpretation if it lacks support in the statute’s text.
